body:
The auto-update toggle could turn itself off. Its on/off state lived only in the in-memory `ServiceState.isRunning` singleton, so an OS process kill reset it to `false` and resuming relied entirely on `START_STICKY`'s restart — which One UI does not reliably honor. The service stayed dead and the toggle showed off until the user tapped Start again.

This persists the intent to DataStore (`auto_update_enabled`): `true` when the timer loop starts, `false` on an explicit Stop. On Home `ViewModel` creation it reconciles the in-memory flag from the persisted intent and revives the service when it should be running — the screen is foregrounded then, so the foreground-service start is allowed.

**Trade-off / known limitation:** reconciliation runs on `ViewModel` creation (a fresh open), not on a warm resume where the `ViewModel` already exists. On an existing install the flag isn't persisted until the loop runs once after updating. In both cases the worst case is simply the previous behavior, not a regression.

title: fix: avoid wallpaper OOM and premature error dismissal
body:
Two independent correctness fixes in `WallpaperService`.

**#55 — OOM risk applying large wallpapers.** `applyWallpaper` decoded the full-resolution bitmap into the app heap via `BitmapFactory.decodeFile` before `setBitmap`. Wallhaven originals are often 4K–8K, so this could OOM on low-RAM devices before the wallpaper was ever applied. It now hands the file to `WallpaperManager.setStream`, letting the framework decode/scale internally — no in-process full-res allocation and no manual `recycle()`.

**#56 — newer error dismissed early.** Each `postError` launched its own coroutine that waited 10s and unconditionally cleared the error, so a second error posted within 10s of the first was wiped by the first one's timer. It now holds the clear job and cancels the outstanding one before scheduling a new clear, so only the most recent error's timer is live.

The coroutine scope is now an overridable `@VisibleForTesting` seam (rather than full Hilt-injected `CoroutineScope`, which would need a qualifier + module for a common type), letting the new `WallpaperServiceErrorTest` drive the #56 race with virtual time. #55 is a framework swap with no pure-JVM test path.

Closes #55
Closes #56

title: Fix offline wallpaper-state persistence and tidy service internals
body:
Code-review findings from a pass over the service/repository layer — two behavioral fixes and a set of cleanups, each in its own commit.

## Fixes
- **Persist wallpaper state on offline cycling and pool applies.** Previously only the online download path wrote the current/previous wallpaper to DataStore via `saveServiceState`; offline cycling (`cycleFromPool`) and manual pool applies (`applySpecificPath`) only mutated the in-memory `ServiceStateRepository`, so the selection was lost after process death. Both paths now persist, matching `HomeViewModel.deleteFromPool`.
- **Cancel the `BootReceiver` coroutine scope** after the boot-start work finishes, instead of leaving a detached scope.

## Cleanups (no behavior change)
- Drop the redundant `poolSize == 0` branch in `onWallpaperFetched` — `trimToSize(0)` already deletes everything and returns an empty list.
- Resolve `NetworkCapabilities` once per `performUpdate` instead of re-fetching `ConnectivityManager` separately in `isOnline()` and `isOnWifi()`.
- Drop the redundant `requireNotNull(response.body)` in `WallpaperFileManager` (already dereferenced non-null above; non-null in OkHttp 5).
- Extract the notification/status timestamp formatting into a named local in `WallpaperService` and `HomeScreen`.

Compiles clean; existing unit-test suite passes. The notification/foreground-service behavior is unchanged.

title: fix: debounce-persist settings text fields
body:
## Summary
- Settings text inputs (search query, aspect ratio, filter color, API key) used to save only on focus loss, so tapping the back arrow while the field still had focus discarded the edit.
- Replaced the focus-loss save with a `PersistOnChange` helper that debounces saves 500ms after the last change and flushes any pending edit on dispose.
- Chip / swatch / Clear-button immediate saves are kept; once upstream catches up, the debounce no-ops.

## Trade-off
Each keystroke now schedules a coroutine-backed save 500ms later. The save path is a cheap DataStore write, so the churn is negligible compared to the UX win of never losing typed input.

title: fix: stop bursting pool downloads after each tick
body:
## Summary

- `WallpaperService.launchPrefetch` used to fetch up to `poolSize` wallpapers back-to-back after every successful update, producing a visible "N at once" burst whenever the pool was below capacity (fresh install, after deleting from the pool, after raising `poolSize`).
- Removed `launchPrefetch`, the `prefetchJob` field, and the now-unused `prefetchJob?.cancel()` / `logger` / `TAG`.
- Pool now grows one wallpaper per timer tick, matching the user-visible "1 per interval" contract. `trimToSize` still caps the pool at `poolSize` on every download.

## Trade-off

Raising `poolSize` mid-flight (e.g., 5 → 25) used to fill on the next tick; it now takes `(new - old)` ticks. Consistent with the rest of the behaviour, accepted as not a regression.

title: fix: restart service after app update
body:
## Summary

- `BootReceiver` only handled `BOOT_COMPLETED`, so installing an app update killed the foreground service with no mechanism to restart it
- Added `MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED` to the receiver's intent filter and updated `onReceive` to accept both actions
- The existing `autoStartOnBoot` guard applies to both cases — service only restarts if the user had it enabled

title: fix(chat): a direct message is no longer copied to the mesh channel
body:
## What was wrong
A message sent in a TAK conversation is also sent over the connected Meshtastic radio, so that people with no server can read it. That copy was made for every conversation. It is a broadcast to the radio channel, written as an "All Chat Rooms" message, so a direct message to one contact was also delivered to everyone on the channel, in their All Chat.

It has been like that since the mesh copy was added in 0.35.1. It needs a radio connected and "Broadcast over mesh" on, which is the default.

## The change
Only the broadcast room, All Chat Users, is copied to the mesh (`ChatConversation.mirrorsToMesh`). A direct message goes to its recipient through the server and nowhere else.

With no server connected, a direct message is now reported as failed. Before, it was shown as sent, because the broadcast had gone out.

## Checked in the app
Android 16 emulator. A stand-in TAK server with one teammate on it, and a simulated radio (Meshtastic firmware 2.7.26) behind a proxy that logs what the app hands to the radio. Message text is never logged, only the shape of each packet.

| Sent in | Build | What the server got | What the radio got |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct message to BRAVO-2 | `main` at 7800974 | chat room "BRAVO-2", addressed to BRAVO-2 | a broadcast to the channel, TAK chat, room "All Chat Rooms" |
| All Chat Users | `main` | chat room "All Chat Rooms", not addressed to one contact | a broadcast to the channel, room "All Chat Rooms" |
| Direct message to BRAVO-2 | this branch | chat room "BRAVO-2", addressed to BRAVO-2 | nothing |
| All Chat Users | this branch | chat room "All Chat Rooms" | a broadcast to the channel, room "All Chat Rooms" |

The same check passed on a build with every Android change merged today plus this one.

## Tests
`ChatMeshMirrorTest`, 6 tests: the broadcast room is mirrored; a direct message is not, with or without a server id; a contact named like the broadcast room does not make its direct message a broadcast; mesh conversations are not mirrored a second time; being a group is not enough. Three deliberate breaks of the rule each fail a test.

The one line in `ChatScreen` that asks the rule has no unit test. The table covers it.

## Not checked
- A physical radio, and a second node receiving.
- MeshCore: a chat event is not sent over MeshCore from a TAK conversation, before or after.

## Known limit
A direct message to a contact who can only be reached over the mesh is not delivered from a TAK conversation. It never was delivered as a direct message. Sending one needs a packet addressed to that contact, which is follow-up work.

title: fix(mesh): a declared length past the buffer ends the message
body:
## What was wrong
`MeshtasticProtoParser.skipField` converted a field's declared length to `Int` before checking it against the buffer. A very large length became negative, so the parser stepped backwards and read the same field again and again.

The TAK packet, ATAK plugin, admin and FromRadio parsers all use `skipField`. A malformed packet could therefore stop mesh processing, and keep one core busy, until the app was restarted.

## The change
The length is now compared, as an unsigned 64-bit value, with what is left in the buffer. A length that runs past the end ends the message. `readLengthDelimited` and `ProtoReader` already did this; `skipField` now does the same.

## Tests
`MeshParsersMalformedInputTest`, 9 tests:
- the helper never moves backwards for any declared length;
- a field with a very large length returns from every parser;
- 200,000 random, structured and crafted inputs per parser, and TAK packets with garbage in their compressed text fields, neither hang nor throw.

Seven of the first eight failed before the change, six of them by timing out.

Also run together with every other change merged today: 1475 tests, 0 failures.

iOS is not affected by this one; its decoder has its own bounds checks.

title: fix(mesh): say when the radio puts a short position interval back to one hour (#257)
body:
Stacked on #248

Fixes #257

One more fix rides along, as its own commits and its own section below: closing an edit transaction that a lost link left open.

**What was wrong (#257).**

A radio at factory settings was sent a position interval of 120 s. The screen said "Sent to the radio: position interval. The radio restarts to save them." and the read-back showed 120. After the restart and a reconnect the field read 3600, the "Sent" line was still there, and nothing said the value had not stuck.

Firmware 2.7.26 (tag v2.7.26.54e0d8d) does this when it loads its config at start, in `NodeDB::NodeDB()` (src/mesh/NodeDB.cpp lines 349 to 365, "Enforce position broadcast minimums if we would send positions over a default channel"):

- The position channel is the first channel, in index order, whose module settings have a `position_precision` other than 0. A channel's role is not looked at.
- When that channel is the default channel, `position_broadcast_secs` is raised to at least one hour, and `broadcast_smart_minimum_interval_secs` to at least five minutes. For the roles ROUTER and ROUTER_LATE the floor is twelve hours (`min_default_broadcast_interval_secs` and `IF_ROUTER`, src/mesh/Default.h lines 21 and 47 to 51). A value of 0 is left alone (`Default::getConfiguredOrMinimumValue`, src/mesh/Default.cpp lines 63 to 70).
- `Channels::isDefaultChannel` (src/mesh/Channels.cpp lines 376 to 388): the key is exactly one byte with the value 1, and the channel's name equals the display name of the modem preset. An empty name stands for that name (`Channels::getName`, lines 358 to 374), and with `use_preset` off the name is "Custom". The display names are those of `DisplayFormatters::getModemPresetDisplayName` (src/DisplayFormatters.cpp): ShortTurbo, ShortSlow, ShortFast, MediumSlow, MediumFast, LongSlow, LongFast, LongTurbo, LongMod, and "Invalid" for a preset with no case there.
- The raised value is saved (the config is compared before and after and written, NodeDB.cpp line 462), so it does not come back.

The radio holds what it is sent until it restarts, which is why the read-back looked right. The stock radio is on its default channel, so every quick pick of the interval control (15, 30, 60, 120, 300 s) is under the floor. #248 saw this on the stock simulator as an interval that was put back after a restart, for a rule that was not known then.

**Fix.**

Two messages, one reason.

Before the push, next to the interval control, when the radio's position channel is its default channel and the interval shown or chosen is above 0 and under the floor for the role:

> This radio sends positions on its public default channel. Meshtastic firmware 2.7.26 raises a position interval under one hour to one hour when the radio restarts. A private channel is needed for faster position updates.

(For a router: "under twelve hours to twelve hours".)

After the restart, once the config download of the same radio is in, the manager compares what the radio reports with what the last push sent, setting by setting, and names each one it did not keep, with both values. With the stock radio and 120 s:

> The radio reports 3600 s for the position interval. 120 s was sent. This radio sends positions on its public default channel. Meshtastic firmware 2.7.26 raises a position interval under one hour to one hour when the radio restarts. A private channel is needed for faster position updates.

The reason is added only when the floor explains the number: the position channel is the default channel, the interval that was sent was above 0 and under the floor for the radio's role, and the radio now reports that floor. A value the radio kept says nothing. The other settings of a push read the same way, for example "The radio reports Client for the role. TAK was sent."

How:

- `PositionFacts` reads what the radio reported (all eight channels, the LoRa config and the device role) from the settings cache, as raw messages, and `onDefaultChannel()` is the firmware's rule. Nothing is decided from the app's own list of saved channels, and a part that is not loaded gives no answer, so nothing is said. The hint also counts what the same push changes (the role, the primary channel's name, the preset), because the firmware decides at the restart, from the radio as it will then be.
- `SentSettings` is what a push sent and which radio it went to, taken from the values the writer wrote (`pushDeviceConfig(edits, onSent)`): the interval in range, the names cut to the firmware's limits, only the settings that were written. The manager keeps it, judges it at every completed download of that radio (`restartNote`), and forgets it when the operator edits or pushes (the screen's existing clear) or a different radio connects (`my_info` with another node number). It survives the link drop that follows a push and the reconnect. The record and the note change under one lock.
- The settings cache announces its changes (`onChange`), and the manager derives `positionFacts` from it.
- Device settings screen: the hint under the interval quick picks, the note under the push result.

**A transaction a lost link left open.**

What the firmware does (src/modules/AdminModule.cpp, 2.7.26): `begin_edit_settings` sets `hasOpenEditTransaction` (line 332), and only `commit_edit_settings` (line 338) or a restart clears it. A client that disconnects does not. While it is set, `saveChanges` neither saves nor restarts (lines 1364 to 1375). Every sequence of the app is begin ... commit, and a sequence left open is closed by the next write, which left this case: the link drops between begin and commit, the operator reconnects and does not push again. The radio keeps the half-finished changes in memory (the screen shows them as the radio's values), nothing is saved, a power cycle silently puts the old values back, and writes from any other client are not saved either.

What the app does: a sequence that ends without its commit is remembered with the radio it went to (node number and `my_info.reboot_count`, field 8, of that link) and with what it had written, each value with what the radio held just before it and what was sent. At the next link-up, after `my_info`:

- Another radio: forgotten, nothing is sent.
- A radio that counts its restarts (either count is not 0): the same count means it has not restarted, so `commit_edit_settings` is the first admin frame the app sends and the result line says the interrupted change was saved and the radio restarts. A different count means the transaction is gone: nothing is sent and the result line says the change was not saved.
- A radio that does not count (both counts 0): firmware 2.7.26 keeps `reboot_count` on ESP32 only (NodeDB.cpp lines 320 to 326 load it under `ARCH_ESP32`; src/platform/esp32/main-esp32.cpp lines 140 to 142 increment it). On the simulator and on nRF52 it is never set, so "unchanged" would be true after a restart too, and a commit to a radio that did restart saves nothing and restarts it a second time. So the app waits for the config download and looks at what the sequence had already written. A written value the radio still reports, that it did not have before the sequence, means its memory survived: commit, and say saved. The old values back means it restarted, or the writes never arrived: send nothing, forget it, say not saved. Nothing written yet: send nothing and forget it; a transaction that is still open is closed by the next push, as before. Written, but nothing the app can compare (an imported channel): send nothing and say to check.

The result line (`lastPushResult`) says:

- saved: "The link dropped while settings were being sent. The radio still held them unsaved, so they were saved now and the radio restarts."
- not saved: "The link dropped while settings were being sent, and the radio does not hold them. That change was not saved."
- cannot tell: "The link dropped while settings were being sent. Check what the radio has, and push again if something is missing."

Until the decision is made no other admin frame goes out: the writer is held (the first admin frame to a radio that counts is the commit, and for one that does not nothing goes out until its download is in). The hold ends when the decision is made, when the link drops (the sequence is kept for the next link-up) or after the settle timeout (the sequence is forgotten). Every kind of sequence reports, not only the Device settings push, and the reported rebroadcast mode is kept in the radio snapshot so that a write of it can be compared too.

Tests: `MeshtasticManagerOpenTransactionTest` (22) drives the app and a `FakeRadio` that follows the firmware's rule (no save and no restart while a transaction is open, a restart loses what was not saved), in the two kinds of radio, each with the radio still running and restarted since:

- a radio that counts, not restarted: the commit is the only frame the app sends, the result line says saved, and the change survives the restart. Restarted: nothing is sent, the result line says not saved, the old value is reported, and the radio is not blamed for "ignoring" the writes.
- a radio that does not count, still holding the change: nothing goes out until the download is in, then the commit. Restarted: nothing is sent and the result line says not saved.
- a value the radio held before the sequence is no evidence; nothing written yet sends nothing (and the next push closes the transaction); one count of the two not being 0 is a count; an imported channel is not guessed at (check); a rebroadcast mode is found in the download like the other settings.
- another radio gets nothing, the sequence is forgotten, and the first radio gets nothing when it comes back.
- a later sequence that commits closes the record, a sequence that committed or never began leaves nothing, and a sequence is judged once, on both kinds of radio.
- a commit refused at the reconnect is tried at the next one, a link that drops while the decision waits keeps the sequence and releases the writer, a download that never completes releases the writer and forgets the sequence.
- no other admin frame goes out ahead of the commit on a slow link, and an operator write started while the decision waits goes out after it.

Also `InterruptedWriteTest` (13), `MyInfoParseTest` (4), `FakeRadioTransactionTest` (4, the fake radio's premises), and 8 more in `MeshSettingsWriterTest` for what a sequence reports, the commit and the hold.

**Checked against a simulated radio (transaction).**

First with a raw TCP script that uses none of the app's code (owner names only, put back byte for byte afterwards, one TCP client at a time), against firmware 2.7.26:

- begin, set_owner, disconnect, reconnect: the new name reads back, so the change is in memory and the transaction survived the client. A container restart with no commit: the old name is back.
- begin, set_owner, disconnect, reconnect, then commit_edit_settings from the new connection: the radio saved and restarted by itself, and the name survived a further container restart.
- begin, disconnect, reconnect, then a plain set_owner from the new connection: the link was still open 30 s later (no restart), the name reads back, and after a container restart the previously saved name was back, so the write was not saved. The control, the same plain write with nothing open: the link dropped 7.3 s later and the name persisted.
- `my_info` on the simulator carries fields 1, 11 and 15 only, before and after every restart: no `reboot_count`, as the source says.

Then the app, `SimRadioSettingsIT.an_interrupted_sequence_is_closed_or_given_up_on_at_the_next_link_up`, with one manager across the reconnects (passed, 2 minutes 28 seconds in the last run):

- A rename whose commit never goes out: the radio reported the new name, unsaved. The manager connected again, found the name in the download, committed and said "The link dropped while settings were being sent. The radio still held them unsaved, so they were saved now and the radio restarts." After the restart the name was saved.
- The same again, then an admin reboot that does not commit: the name was gone. The manager connected again, found the old name, sent nothing and said "The link dropped while settings were being sent, and the radio does not hold them. That change was not saved." Fifteen seconds later the link was still up, so no stray commit had restarted the radio a second time, and no "did not take" note had appeared.

The radio read as it did at the start when the test finished.

**Tests.**

Counts: 1278 tests in 125 classes at the head of #248, 1409 in 132 classes with this change, 0 failures, 12 skipped (9 skipped on main, plus the three opt-in simulated radio tests). `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug` builds.

New classes: `PositionFactsTest` (23), `SentSettingsTest` (13), `MeshtasticManagerPositionFloorTest` (22), `MeshtasticManagerOpenTransactionTest` (22), `InterruptedWriteTest` (13), `MyInfoParseTest` (4), `FakeRadioTransactionTest` (4). Extended, with the totals now: `DeviceSettingsStateTest` (34), `MeshSettingsWriterTest` (55), `RadioSettingsCacheTest` (19), `SentLedgerTest` (10). `FakeRadio` gained `restart()` (the firmware's position floor, written from the source and not from the app's reading of it), `stock()`, `download()`, the firmware's rule for edit transactions and a reboot count for a radio that counts restarts. `RadioApp` wires the app and a fake radio the way the application does.

The #257 cases, each through the manager and the settings state: default channel and 120 s (the hint; after the reconnect the note with both numbers and the reason); a primary channel with a 32 byte key (no hint, value kept, no note); a name that is not the preset's on the default key (not the default channel, which is what the firmware does and the simulator confirmed); the preset's own name written out (it is); position precision 0 on every channel; an interval of 0; routers (roles 2 and 11) and the roles that are not; a role, a rename or a preset chosen in the same push; a different radio after the push (no note, and none when the first radio comes back); the note stays through link drops and reconnects and goes with the next edit or push; a download that leaves a setting out; a push that did not reach the radio; the facts follow what the radio reported, are empty while a download is half in, and the link drop empties them.

To check that the new tests notice a regression, I broke the code one change at a time, and each time at least one test failed: 52 ways for #257 and 42 for the transaction.

For #257: the firmware's rule (the floor, the router roles, which channel is the position channel, the key, the name, `use_preset`, the preset names, a channel or the LoRa config that is not loaded, a rename or preset of the same push standing in); the hint (an interval of 0 or at the floor, the role, the rename and the preset of the same push, data not loaded); the note (the reason without the default channel, without the floor being what is reported, for an interval of 0 or one over the floor, the values swapped, a kept value named, the order, the reason dropped, the router floor); the manager (not judged when the download completes, a different radio not forgotten, the edit or push not clearing, a new push not clearing, a link drop clearing, a download not starting from nothing, the push not remembered, the facts not refreshed); the writer and the cache.

For the transaction: the count not read, or read from another field; a sequence that never reports a transaction left open, reports one it never began, or records a commit that went out as not sent; the value before not read; the written values or settings not reported; the commit not sent; the hold missing from a sequence, from a read or from the manager, or applied to the commit itself; a different radio not forgotten, or judged from its download; the count compared the wrong way, a restart not said, one count of the two not being a count; nothing written decided from the download; the download not waited for, or the decision not made; memory that survived not committed, memory that is gone committed or not said, nothing comparable not said; the record kept after the commit went out, forgotten when the commit did not go out, or not closed by a later commit; the count not remembered; a dropped link not releasing the writer; a download that never completes holding it; the verdict taking a value held before as evidence, nothing comparable as gone, or any change as evidence; the rebroadcast mode not compared or not kept; the ledger not cleared of the sequence, or clearing every radio. One of the 42 was not caught at first, the record kept after the commit went out, and a test was added for it.

The lock that keeps the note and the record of the last push from racing with an edit has no test: a race cannot be made to happen on purpose here.

**Checked against a simulated radio (#257).**

`SimRadioSettingsIT.a_short_position_interval_on_the_default_channel_is_raised_and_the_app_says_so` runs against meshtasticd, firmware 2.7.26, through the app's own TCP client, parser, cache, settings state and writer, with one manager across the restart as in the app:

    MESHSIM_HOST=<host> ./gradlew :app:cleanTestDebugUnitTest :app:testDebugUnitTest --console=plain --max-workers=3 --tests '*SimRadioSettingsIT.a_short_position*'

It passed (4 minutes 15 seconds in the last run), and the radio read exactly as it did at the start when the test finished. The whole class (`--tests '*SimRadioSettingsIT*'`: the test of #248 and the two new ones) passed on the final code in 14 minutes 16 seconds. The test of #248 now shows the rule in its own log: its first step reads "the restart reset the position interval" on the stock radio, and "the restart kept the position interval" in every step after it has put a private key on the primary channel. Four radios in a row, each the stock radio with something changed on its primary channel (key lengths only, never the key):

- A. The stock radio: `interval=3600 smart_min_interval=300 channel0[key_length=1 name='' precision=13] preset=0 role=0`. The hint for 120 s was shown. Right after the write the radio reported `interval=120`. After the restart, `interval=3600`, and the manager that made the push said "The radio reports 3600 s for the position interval. 120 s was sent." followed by the reason.
- B. A 32 byte key on the primary channel (`key_length=32`, interval 3600 before): no hint. Right after the write `interval=120`, after the restart `interval=120`, no note.
- C. The default key with the name "Alpha": after the restart that followed the channel change the radio held `interval=120` still, the firmware does not call it the default channel, and the app said nothing.
- D. The default key with the preset's name "LongFast" and no position precision on any channel: after the restart `interval=120` still, and the app said nothing.

**Not verified.**

- No physical radio and no phone were used. The BLE path is untouched and was not run: the reconnect after a restart (the BLE client reconnects by itself) goes through the same `my_info` and download handling as TCP.
- Only firmware 2.7.26 was read and measured. The hint is decided from the radio's channels, LoRa config and role, not from its firmware version, which the app does not read. Its wording names 2.7.26 and claims nothing about other versions.
- The hint and the note are two `Text` lines on the Device settings screen. The screen was not run in the app, so their look and placement are unseen. What they say is decided in `DeviceSettingsState.positionIntervalHint`, `SentSettings` and the manager, which the tests drive.
- The note and the record of the last push are kept in memory: they are lost if the app is killed before the radio is back. The record of an interrupted sequence is too: if the app is killed before it reconnects, the transaction stays open until the next write, as

title: fix(mesh): settings writes reach the radio and change only what was edited (#240)
body:
Fixes #240
Refs #185

**What was wrong.**

Several faults, each hiding the next.

1. Every admin frame wrote `Data.want_response` to field 5. In mesh.proto field 5 is `source`, a fixed32, so the firmware's decoder rejected the frame (`wrong wire type`) and the radio logged `ignore malformed toradio`. On firmware 2.7.26 no settings write and no read-back request from this app reached the radio's admin module. The first commit moves it to field 3.

2. With frames accepted, the setters were destructive. The firmware replaces a whole config, channel or owner with what a write carries, and each builder sent only the field it changed, so every other field went back to its default. Measured against firmware 2.7.26 on a simulated radio, with the field 3 framing:
   - LoRa preset: region US to UNSET, hop limit 5 to 0, transmit on to off, boosted gain on to off
   - channel 0 rename: key length 32 to 0, position precision 13 to 0
   - position interval: GPS mode ENABLED to DISABLED, position flags 811 to 0, smart broadcast off, GPS update interval 120 to 0
   - device role or rebroadcast mode: time zone cleared, LED switch reset
   - owner rename: the licensed flag true to false

3. Frames sent back to back lost writes. The firmware keeps four inbound packets for its router thread and drops the oldest when a fifth arrives, without telling the sender. In a batch of six frames the device config write never took effect, and in a batch of seven the position config write did not. The twelve read requests of `requestDeviceConfig`, sent back to back, got four answers.

4. What the app chose to write was wrong, and what it said afterwards was not always true.
   - A radio at its factory defaults reports no role and no channel name, because proto3 leaves out a field that holds its default. The parser read the missing role as unknown, and the store kept the draft's own value instead: a fresh install's TAK and "OmniTAK", a name left by an earlier push, or whatever another radio had left. The push compared that draft with the radio and wrote the difference. Changing only the position interval also changed the role and renamed the primary channel, which changes its frequency slot and takes the radio off the air.
   - An admin message from any node could change the draft, because the radio hands the phone every admin message addressed to it.
   - A write was patched onto what the app had cached when the link came up. A channel key rotated by another client would be put back by the next rename, and a position write patched onto bytes read before a role change would undo the defaults the firmware installs for the new role.
   - After a write the cache held what was sent, as if the radio had taken it. A managed radio ignores local admin, and the app said "Pushed" and then "Nothing to change". A single write ran outside `begin_edit_settings` and `commit_edit_settings`, so a transaction left open by a dropped link stayed open.
   - A read-back was believed when it came from our own node number, and a write's read took the next frame for its entry.
   - A radio whose position interval another client had set above a day showed "position interval" as edited on connect, because the screen compared a draft clamped to a day with the radio's own value, and any push of another setting rewrote the interval to a day.
   - The Device settings screen sent its twelve reads as soon as the link was up, while the radio was still streaming its config download.
   - The 3 second wait for an answer was measured over TCP, and a refusal for no answer said the radio might be managed.
   - On the Mesh Channels screen the region control started at US, so applying a preset to a radio in Europe set its region to US. An imported channel was written to the slot at its row's index, so the first one replaced the primary channel (name, key, precision). The node number of the last radio outlived the link, so a frame could be addressed to a radio that was no longer there.

**Fix.**

The patch core. Every setter sends the radio's own message with one field changed.

- `ProtoFields` reads a message as its top-level fields (number, wire type, exact bytes) and patches them: replace, insert or remove a field, or a field of a nested message. Fields this app has never heard of come back byte for byte in their original order. Input it cannot read gives null.
- `RadioSettingsCache` holds what the radio reported, as raw bytes: the device, position and LoRa configs by their oneof number, each channel by index, and the radio's own User. It is fed by the config download, whose frames are not mesh packets, and by the answers that pass the read-back rule below. It takes no mesh packet by itself. It is emptied when the link drops and when the next download's `my_info` arrives.
- Only what the app patches is kept. The security config (the radio's private key) and the network config (its Wi-Fi password) are dropped as they arrive, because nothing in the app writes them. A channel does hold its key, because a rename has to carry it back unchanged. `toString` shows counts only.
- The setters (device role, rebroadcast mode, position interval, LoRa preset and region, channel 0 name, owner names) take one entry, change their one field, and return null for bytes they cannot read. A region of `UNSET` and a null preset leave the radio's own as they are. None of them builds a message from scratch.
- The frames of a sequence go out 100 ms apart. A channel name is cut to the firmware's 11 bytes on a character boundary, as owner names already are.

What a read-back has to be.

A write patches what the radio says it holds, so what counts as the radio saying so is checked, not assumed. An admin message is taken as a read-back only when it is the radio's own answer to a read this app sent:

- every get request carries a fresh random non-zero packet id, kept as outstanding with the entry it asked for (config type, channel index or owner) and a deadline (`AdminReads`)
- the answer is from our own node and quotes that id in `Data.request_id`, for the same entry
- it carries none of the marks a radio puts on a packet it received from outside: a signal strength (`rx_rssi`), a signal to noise ratio (`rx_snr`), `via_mqtt`, or a transport other than its own (`transport_mechanism`)
- an id is used once and expires with its deadline. Anything else is ignored, with one log line that names the reason and never the payload
- a write's read waits for the answer to its own request, not for the next frame for that entry
- `rx_time` and `hop_start` are not part of the rule: a radio with a clock puts `rx_time` on its own answers, and what other firmware puts in either field on its own packets was not measured, so a rule that used them could refuse every write
- the config download frames (`FromRadio.config`, `FromRadio.channel`, `my_info` and the node info for our own node) are not mesh packets and are taken as before. Nothing else reaches the cache, the settings state or the "did not take" check

Measured against firmware 2.7.26 on a simulated radio: the answer to a local read quotes the request's packet id for the owner, the device, position and LoRa configs and every channel, and carries none of those marks and no `hop_start`. `rx_time` is absent while the radio has no clock and present on every answer once it has one. Another firmware that does not quote the request id in its local answers would refuse every write rather than patch the wrong bytes. That was not found on 2.7.26 and could not be checked on other versions.

What gets written.

- An absent field decodes as its proto3 default: role CLIENT, rebroadcast ALL, preset LONG_FAST, interval 0, name "". A number the app has no name for decodes as unknown and is never written.
- `DeviceSettingsState` holds the draft the screen edits and `radio`, what the connected radio last reported (null when nothing is loaded or the link is down). A setting counts as edited only when `radio` has it and the draft differs. A report updates `radio`, and updates the draft for every setting that is not edited. When `radio` was null the report overwrites the draft, so nothing carries over from an earlier radio or session. When the link drops, `radio` goes back to null.
- `pushDeviceConfig` takes the edited settings only (`DeviceEdits`), role first. A value that differs only because the radio changed is not written. Before a push the screen says "Will send to the radio: position interval"; afterwards it says "Sent to the radio: position interval". The push button is off when nothing is edited.
- Reports reach the store only from the config download and from answers that pass the read-back rule. The radio's own node info supplies the owner names, and the node number is forgotten when the link drops.
- The position interval is compared with the radio's own value as it is. A radio set above a day by another client shows its real value and is not "edited", and a push of another setting leaves the interval alone. The interval is clamped to a day only when the operator changed it, and the store no longer clamps the draft.

How it is written.

- Each entry is requested from the radio just before it is patched, with a packet id of its own. The writer waits for the answer to that request, 3 seconds over TCP and 8 over Bluetooth, and patches those bytes. With no answer nothing is changed and the result says the radio did not answer. It does not say why: a managed radio looks the same from here as a slow link.
- The role goes first, so the entries after it are read after the firmware has installed the role's defaults. Settings are written one at a time.
- Every sequence, a single write included, runs between `begin_edit_settings` and `commit_edit_settings`, so a transaction left open by a dropped link is closed by the next write. The transaction opens only when there is something to write, and once open it is always committed, even after a failure and even if the screen that started it goes away.
- `requestDeviceConfig` takes the same lock and spacing as the writes. Its twelve reads wait for `config_complete_id` and for the link to be quiet for 400 ms, so they do not land in the middle of the config download. The quiet wait ends 2 seconds after the download and the whole wait after 20, so a busy mesh cannot hold them, and it ends at once when the link drops or no radio is attached. The read on connect and the read-back after a push both go through it. The read on connect is kept: it refreshes what the screen holds when the screen is opened long after the download.

What the operator is told.

- Written entries are dropped from the cache instead of being replaced by what was sent. The radio's next report fills them with what it kept.
- `SentLedger` remembers what was sent to each node. When that radio next reports the setting with a different value, the screen says "The radio did not take: role. It may be managed." Each entry is judged once and expires after ten minutes.
- A sequence that stops partway says what was sent and what was not. If the link drops between begin and commit, it says some settings may have been applied and to reconnect and check what the radio has. It does not say they did not reach the radio once the commit has gone out.
- A push ends with the radio restarting, and over TCP the link drops with it. The manager keeps what the last push said (`lastPushResult`) next to the "did not take" note, so both stay on the Device settings screen while the link is down, after it comes back and after the screen is left. The screen clears them when the operator edits a field or pushes again. Reports from the radio also move the draft, but they are not edits and leave the result alone.

Mesh Channels.

- The region and preset controls start at what the radio reported, and Apply sends only what the operator picked and changed. A region the operator did not pick is never written. With no LoRa config reported the button is off.
- An imported channel goes into the first free secondary slot, found by reading slots 1 to 7 from the radio. With none free nothing is written and the screen says so. The primary is replaced only through a separate "Replace primary" button, after a confirmation. The imported name is cut to 11 bytes.
- In a channel row the text has the card's full width and the buttons sit on their own row beneath it, wrapping onto a second line on a narrow screen.

**Tests.**

New classes: `ProtoFieldsTest` (36), `AdminReadModifyWriteTest` (34), `RadioSettingsCacheTest` (16), `MeshtasticProtoParserRawBytesTest` (7), `MeshSettingsWriterTest` (43), `MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest` (23), `MeshtasticManagerReadBackTest` (12), `MeshtasticManagerSettleTest` (6), `AdminReadsTest` (18), `DeviceSettingsStateTest` (22), `AdminResponseDefaultsTest` (12), `SentLedgerTest` (9), `LoraPicksTest` (9) and `SimRadioSettingsIT` (1, skipped unless `MESHSIM_HOST` is set). `MeshtasticMeshPacketFieldsTest` gained four tests for the request id, `via_mqtt` and `transport_mechanism`. `FakeRadio` is a test helper that behaves like the firmware for admin messages: it answers reads, quoting the request's packet id, replaces a whole config or channel on a write, takes the owner names and the licensed flag from `set_owner`, and can be made to ignore everything, as a managed radio does. Five existing classes (`AdminAddressingTest`, `ChannelApplyEncoderTest`, `MeshWireToRadioFieldsTest`, `OwnerNameClampTest`, `PositionBroadcastFieldTest`) were updated for the new builder signatures. They hand the builders an empty message as the one the radio reported, so the byte layouts they pin are unchanged.

Each case from the review is a test:

- a factory radio with a fresh-install draft and one edited field is exactly one write, and the role and channel name are not touched (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`, `MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest`, `DeviceSettingsStateTest`)
- a draft left by radio A does not carry over when radio B connects (`DeviceSettingsStateTest`)
- an admin message or node info from another node changes neither the cache nor the store (`MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest`, `MeshtasticManagerReadBackTest`, `RadioSettingsCacheTest`)
- a setting that changed on the radio but was not edited follows the radio and is not written (`DeviceSettingsStateTest`)
- a role or preset the app has no name for is never written (`DeviceSettingsStateTest`, `AdminResponseDefaultsTest`)
- the role is written first, and the position entry is read again after it (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`)
- a channel key rotated by another client is not put back by a rename (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`)
- the cache does not become what was sent, and a radio that kept its own value is named after its next report (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`, `SentLedgerTest`, `MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest`)
- a single write is inside begin and commit, a transaction left open is closed by the next write, a begun sequence is committed after a failure, and a link that drops before the commit is worded as "may have been applied" (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`)
- `requestDeviceConfig` waits for a write in progress and spaces its requests (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`, `MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest`)
- a preset-only apply keeps the radio's region, a region the operator did not pick is never sent, and with no LoRa config there is nothing to apply (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`, `LoraPicksTest`)
- an import goes into the first free secondary slot, the primary only on request, the name is cut to 11 bytes, and a full radio refuses (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`)
- the node number is forgotten when the link drops, over a real TCP socket as well (`MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest`)
- what a push said is kept until it is cleared for the next edit or push, stays through the link drop and the download after it together with the "did not take" note, is kept for a refused push too, and is recorded when the screen that started the push is left (`MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest`)
- a security or network config frame is not retained, however it arrives: fed to the cache directly, through a config download, as a mesh packet, and as an answer to a read, which is not an entry at all (`RadioSettingsCacheTest`, `MeshtasticManagerRadioSettingsTest`, `AdminReadsTest`)
- an answer with the right sender but no request id, with a wrong id, with the id of a read for another entry, or with the right id and any one of the marks of a received packet in turn is ignored, a used id and an expired id are ignored, `rx_time` and `hop_start` do not matter, and reads of an earlier session are not answered in the next one (`MeshtasticManagerReadBackTest`, `AdminReadsTest`)
- a frame that is not the radio's answer does not end the read of a write and the genuine answer after it does, and an older answer for the same entry does not end a newer read (`MeshtasticManagerReadBackTest`, `MeshSettingsWriterTest`)
- a radio at three days shows no edit, a role-only push leaves its interval alone on the fake radio (`DeviceSettingsStateTest`, `MeshSettingsWriterTest`) and on the simulated one (`SimRadioSettingsIT`), and a changed interval is sent in range
- the reads of a refresh wait for the end of the download and for a quiet link, give up when the link drops, and are bounded (`MeshtasticManagerSettleTest`)
- a read waits 8 seconds instead of 3 over Bluetooth, and a timeout says the radio did not answer, never that it is managed (`MeshSettingsWriterTest`)

    ./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest --console=plain -q --max-workers=3

Counts: 1019 tests on main, 1278 in 125 classes with this change, 0 failures, 10 skipped (9 skipped on main, plus the opt-in simulated radio test). `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug` builds.

To check that the new tests notice a regression, I broke the code 28 ways in the earlier rounds and 32 more in this one, one change at a time, and each time at least one test failed. The earlier ones were run again on the final code. Two no longer had anything to break and were replaced: the check on who an admin message is from by the sender mutation below, and the patch from cached bytes by two others (a write that patches the cached copy without a fresh read, and one that falls back to the cached copy when no answer comes). All were caught.

In this round:

- the read-back rule: the sender not checked, each of `rx_rssi`, `rx_snr`, `via_mqtt` and `transport_mechanism` not checked in turn, a request id of zero accepted, any request id accepted, the entry not matched to the request, an id not used up by its answer, the deadline ignored, ids that may be zero or repeat, config variants the app does not keep read as answers, a write's read ending on the cache instead of its own answer, the manager not storing the answer or not handing it to the waiting read, the cache taking admin packets again, the parser dropping the request id, `via_mqtt` or `transport_mechanism`, and reads of an earlier session surviving
- the interval: compared after clamping, a report that clamps the draft, an unchanged interval sent anyway, a changed interval sent out of range
- the read timeout and its wording: Bluetooth getting the TCP timeout, the writer ignoring the link's timeout, a timeout blamed on a managed radio
- the settle wait: reads that do not wait for the download, no wait for a quiet link, a new download that does not reset the wait, a wait that goes on after the link drops, the end of the download not noticed

Earlier rounds:

- what gets written: an absent field decoded as unknown, a report that never moves the unedited draft, a role the app cannot name overwritten by the draft, a link drop that keeps the old radio snapshot, an admin message accepted from any node, a node info accepted from any node
- reading first: a patch that starts from the cached bytes, the role written last
- what the operator is told: the cache taking what was sent, sent values not remembered, a radio that kept its value never reported, a ledger entry judged more

title: fix(meshcore): a dropped marker no longer moves the radio's advertised position (#234)
body:
Fixes #234.

## What was wrong
With a MeshCore radio connected, `MeshCoreManager.sendCoTOverMesh` treated every CoT event that was not chat as the operator's own position. It wrote the event's coordinates into the radio's advert (SET_ADVERT_LATLON) and broadcast the advert (SEND_SELF_ADVERT).

The map screen calls it for every marker the operator drops or saves, for FEMA palette markers and for military reports. So each of those told the MeshCore mesh that the operator was standing on the marker, until the app next sent the operator's real position. With "broadcast over mesh" off, nothing would have corrected it.

The server to mesh relay had the same hazard and was switched off for MeshCore in #231. The marker paths were left.

## The change
- `MeshFrameworkManager.sendCoTOverMesh` takes `ownPosition`, false unless the caller says otherwise. The position broadcaster is the one caller that sets it.
- MeshCore sends a position only when it is set. A marker, a report or a relayed contact sends nothing there: the advert is the only place MeshCore has for a position, and it is this radio's own.
- Meshtastic ignores the flag and sends what it sent before.
- What goes on the wire is decided in one plain function, `MeshCoreManager.outboundFrames`, so it is tested without a radio.

Nothing an operator could use is lost. A marker dropped while MeshCore is the active mesh still goes to the TAK servers and stays on the local map. It never reached MeshCore peers as a marker.

## Tests
`MeshCoreOutboundTest`, 7 tests on the frames themselves:
- the operator's own position gives SET_ADVERT_LATLON with its coordinates, then SEND_SELF_ADVERT;
- a dropped marker gives nothing, and neither does a saved marker, a FEMA marker, a military report, a hostile track, a spot, a waypoint or somebody else's position report;
- the event type does not make a position the operator's own, only the caller does;
- chat is never an advert;
- an own position the radio cannot hold sends nothing, and no advert broadcast either;
- a caller that does not pass the flag is not sending an own position (this pins the default on the interface).

Six deliberate breaks of those rules each fail a test: the guard removed, the default flipped, chat let through, the broadcast dropped, the two frames swapped, the broadcast sent without coordinates.

Suite: 1026 tests, 0 failures (1019 on `main`).

## Not checked
- No MeshCore radio was used, before or after. What the app sent before is read from the code on `main`, and what it sends now from the frames the tests build. What a second MeshCore node shows for those frames is taken from the companion protocol, not seen.
- The one line in `OmniTAKApp` that passes `ownPosition = true` for the position broadcaster has no unit test. Without it MeshCore position sharing would stop, which a radio check would show at once.
- iOS does not have this path: its marker drops go to Meshtastic only.

title: fix(map): survive Activity rebuilds, stop recentering on return, and three more faults of the kept map view (#251 to #254)
body:
Fixes #251, #252, #253 and #254. All four come from the one map view the app keeps for the whole process (`RetainedMapView`, #177), and all four are in every release from 0.40.0 to 0.45.0.

## What was wrong

**1. The app crashed whenever Android rebuilt the Activity while the app kept running (#251).**
`TacticalMap` forwarded `ON_DESTROY` to `mapView.onDestroy()`. The destroyed view stayed in the holder, so the next Activity was handed a view with no style and no native map, whose location component still reported "activated". The first call that reached the location layer threw `IllegalStateException: Calling getSourceAs when a newer style is loading/has loaded`.

That happens on a system dark mode switch (so also Battery Saver and a scheduled dark theme), a font or display size change, a language change, the app swiped out of Recents and reopened while the connection service keeps the process alive, and Back followed by a reopen where Back finishes the Activity. #197 has the same exception from another call into the location component and looks like the same fault. The guard added there left the next unguarded call to throw.

**2. Returning to the Map tab moved the camera back to your own position at zoom 15 (#252, which is #7 again).**
The "Center on me" effect acted on the trigger value the map was composed with. On the kept view that starts a camera move at once, so every return recentered.

**3. After one visit to another tab the map screen had no map (#253).**
`MapScreen` keeps the `MapLibreMap` handle in composition state and only the factory that builds the view ever delivered it. Every later composition held null: Offline maps said "Pan the map to the area you want, then reopen this sheet." wherever the map was, and overlay changes, "zoom to overlay", lasso and plugin map overlays did nothing until the app was restarted.

**4. After the first visit to another tab, a style reload redrew old data (#254).**
The listener registered with `addOnDidFinishLoadingStyleListener` lives as long as the view but read state of the composition that built it. After that composition was gone, every 3D terrain or basemap change put back the drawings, measurement and grid as they were at that moment.

## The change

- **The view is never destroyed with its host.** Nothing forwards `ON_DESTROY`. The view is kept and the next Activity shows it, which is what `RetainedMapView` always said it did.
- **Only the composition that took the view last may drive it.** When an Activity is finished and opened again, the new one is created before the old one has been stopped and destroyed, so for a moment two compositions hold the view. Each composition has a holder token. `RetainedMapView.acquire` records it, and lifecycle forwarding, writing `bindings` and the dispose-time detach all check it. Without this the old Activity's late `onStop` freezes the map the new one is showing, and its dispose pulls the view out of the new screen.
- **The detach has its own effect, keyed on the view.** It sat in the lifecycle effect, which also restarts when navigation gives a destination a new back stack entry.
- **The composable's location component calls go through one guard** (`withReadyLocationComponent`): a loaded style, an activated component, and a caught `IllegalStateException`. Recenter and follow-me wait for a style when there is none, and that wait lapses when the press is superseded or the map leaves the screen.
- **Composing the map onto the existing view is not a recenter request.** A press is. The composition that builds the view still opens on your position, marker shown or hidden, so a cold start behaves as before. That is decided when the map is ready, from the state at that moment.
- **Every composition is handed the map**, and the four overlay effects in `MapScreen` are keyed on the handle so they run when it arrives. KML shapes that are already drawn on that map are not read from disk and parsed again.
- **The style reload listener reads `RetainedMapView.bindings`** and the application context. Each pass writes that state in its first effect, before any later effect can reload the style.
- **The map screen starts from the preferences the app has already read**, not from one pass of defaults. On the kept view that pass reloaded the style to the default basemap and back on every return for anyone not on Topo.
- The callbacks in `bindings` are cleared when the map leaves the screen, so a view nobody is showing does not keep that composition reachable.

The decisions are plain functions (`RetainedSlot`, `RetainedMapRules`, `KmlShapeRenderer.needsApply`) so they can be tested without a `MapView`.

## Checked in the app

Android 16 emulator, debug builds of `main` at 7800974 ("before") and of this branch, same saved settings, location on, connected to a stand-in TAK server so the connection service is running. One script ran both.

| Scenario | Before | This branch |
|---|---|---|
| Dark mode on, then off, map open | crash on the first switch | same process through both rebuilds, map moves |
| Back, wait 4 s, reopen, 6 rounds | crash on each of the 3 reopens that followed a Back from the running app | 6 of 6 survived |
| Back and reopen at once, 6 rounds | 2 crashes | 6 of 6 survived. In all 6 the new Activity was created before the old one was destroyed |
| Task removed while connected (what a Recents swipe does), reopen | crash on open | same process, map moves |
| Font size 1.15, then 1.0 | crash on the first change | same process through both rebuilds, map moves |
| Home and back, screen off and on | fine | fine |
| Pan away, open Settings, return to Map | own marker back in the middle of the screen | marker where it was left |
| Offline maps sheet after one visit to Settings | "Pan the map to the area you want..." | source and tile count |
| Range rings at A, tab switch, rings at B, switch 3D terrain | rings drawn at A, banner says B | rings at B |
| Center on me | recenters | recenters |
| Cold start with the map left panned away, marker shown (5 and 4 runs) | opens on own position | opens on own position |
| The same with "My marker" off (4 runs each) | opens on own position | opens on own position |
| "My marker" off: pan away, Settings and back, then Center on me | not run | camera stays, then recenters |
| Chat, then Map again 0.05 to 0.8 s later | map fine | map fine |
| Satellite basemap with the triangle marker, and with "My marker" off: Settings and back | marker as set | marker as set |

## Review

Two independent reviews, each of the version before it. What they changed:

- Cold start had stopped opening on your own position, first with the marker shown and then, after that was restored, with the marker hidden. Both were measured on `main`, restored, and are in the table.
- The style listener read state written one pass late. That did not show up in the app (the marker row passes on both builds), but the order is now exact.
- The detach could in principle run when only the lifecycle owner changed. The second review showed navigation never does that here; the detach has its own effect anyway.
- Handing the map to every composition made the KML shape renderer read and parse its files on every return to the map, hence the skip, which forgets a draw that failed.

## Tests

`RetainedMapViewTest` (14) and three new cases in `KmlShapeRendererTest`: the view is built once and survives a release, only the last holder holds it, a replaced holder cannot release it, nothing is forwarded for `ON_DESTROY` or by a replaced composition, composing onto an existing view is not a recenter request, building the view is one, and a press is told apart from both, clearing the callbacks keeps the state a style reload needs, unchanged KML shapes are not drawn again. Twelve deliberate breaks of the holder, lifecycle and recenter rules each fail a test. Suite: 1036 tests, 0 failures.

The wiring inside the composable has no unit test, and neither has the crash itself. The table is what covers them.

## Not checked, and limits

- No physical phone yet. Everything above is one emulator.
- Follow-me could not be exercised: with Follow on, this emulator's graphics layer crashes inside its own GL library within seconds, on `main` as well. Follow did turn the camera to the marker once on an earlier build of this branch before that happened.
- After returning to the Map tab the emulator leaves a black strip at the bottom of the map once the tab bar hides, on `main` as well. Not caused by this change. Whether a phone does it has not been checked.
- Battery Saver, a scheduled dark theme and a language change were not tried one by one. They rebuild the Activity the same way a dark mode switch does.
- The view now really does live as long as the process. The location component keeps the Activity that first showed the map reachable: one Activity, not one per rebuild.
- MapLibre reads the display density once, when the view is built. After a display size change the map keeps its old scale for symbols and the marker until the app is restarted. Before this change that rebuild crashed.
- With a large KML file the first load still parses on the main thread, as it did. Only the repeat on every return is gone.
- After a cold start in 3D globe mode, the first switch to the 2D map still goes to your position. Before this change every such switch did.

title: fix(map): range rings banner keeps its Clear and Done buttons on a phone
body:
## What was wrong

On a phone, the range rings banner had no usable buttons.

- Waiting for a tap ("Range rings · tap map to set center"): Clear was squeezed into a strip 36 px wide with its label broken over two lines, and Done was not there.
- With rings placed ("Rings lat, lon · 100m · 500m · 1.0km · 2.0km · 5.0km"): neither Clear nor Done existed.

So the tool could not be closed from its own banner. The rings and the banner stayed until another tool was started or the Map tab was left.

The banner is a `Row` of the readout text and two `TextButton`s. The text had no weight, so it was measured first with the whole row width and the buttons got what was left, which was nothing.

## The change

`Modifier.weight(1f, fill = false)` on the readout text in `RangeRingsOverlay`, and the same on `MeasurementOverlay`, which has the same layout (its text is shorter, so it only showed at larger font sizes or on narrow screens). The buttons keep their size and the text wraps in the space that is left. The banner still only grows as wide as it needs.

## Checked in the app

Android 16 emulator, 1080 px wide, default font size, before and after on the same screen:

| State | 0.45.0 code | This branch |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting for a tap | Clear 36 px wide, no Done | Clear and Done |
| Rings placed | no buttons | Clear and Done |

On this branch Clear takes the rings off and waits for a new center, and Done closes the tool and removes the rings.

## Not checked

- A physical phone, a tablet, landscape, larger font sizes.
- The measurement banner was not opened; it got the same one-line change.

title: fix(uas): Follow-Me waits for a live fix, not one restored from the last session (#235)
body:
Fixes #235

**What was wrong.** `UASManager.startFollowMe()` took the operator's position from `LocationProvider.fix` whatever it was. At a cold start that is the fix restored from the last session (#205): where the operator was then, possibly far from where they are now. Follow-Me would engage and send that position to the vehicle once a second until a live fix replaced it.

**Fix.** A restored fix does not count as a position to follow. Follow-Me answers "no GPS fix" (the operator sees "Need your GPS fix first") until a live one arrives, exactly as when there is no fix at all. The altitude fallback still reads the fix as before: a restored altitude is a better guess than none.

**Tests.** `UASManagerFollowMeTest`, 4 tests: a restored fix is refused; no fix is refused; a live fix gets past the position check (the test has no vehicle, so the answer is "not connected"); a live fix that replaces a restored one is accepted. `./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest --tests '*UASManagerFollowMeTest*'` passes; CI runs the full suite.

**Not verified.** No vehicle and no simulator: this is a check at the start of the follow path, covered by unit tests only.

**Left open.** #249: the follow altitude falls back to sea level when there is neither terrain data nor a fix, and a live fix that stops updating is followed without an age limit. Both were read from the code while doing this and need a decision.

title: fix(servers): notice a dead TAK connection and re-dial (#233)
body:
Fixes #233

**What was wrong.** A TAK connection whose path is gone without a FIN or RST (Wi-Fi to LTE swap, NAT timeout, server host gone) stayed Connected. `TAKConnection` read with no timeout, never asked the server anything, and a failed write returned false without changing the state. The bar stayed green, the send counter kept ticking, and nothing arrived.

**Fix, in `TAKConnection`.**
- While connected, the app sends the standard TAK ping (a CoT of type `t-x-c-t`, which servers answer with `t-x-c-t-r`). The ping carries the device UID with a `-ping` suffix and a 10 s stale time, as other clients' pings do. OpenTAKServer sends the ping itself back instead of a pong; that counts as an answer too.
- Until the server has answered one, a ping goes out every 15 s, busy stream or not. After that, only when nothing has arrived for 15 s.
- A server that has answered a ping is given up on when a ping gets no reply of any kind for 25 s, checked on two 5 s ticks in a row. The connection is then reported Failed and re-dialed. A link is never dropped for idle time alone: a process that was stalled wakes up to a long silence on its clock, and the server was never asked.
- A server that has never answered a ping is not dropped for being quiet. A plain CoT listener that ignores pings would otherwise be reconnected in a loop. That case is #245.
- No ping goes out in the first 15 s of a connection, so the app's own first event reaches the server first. A server that takes a client's identity from the first event it sees must not get the ping for that.
- The watchdog never waits for a write. Pings are written from their own coroutine and sockets are closed off-thread, so a write stuck on a dead path, or a slow TLS close, cannot stop the check that would catch it.
- A failed write ends the connection.
- `connect()` no longer drops a dial that arrives while the previous session is still unwinding. Each session is numbered, and one that has ended or been replaced cannot change the state or the socket of a newer one. A new dial waits at most 2 s for the old session.
- The TLS handshake has a read timeout. A server that accepted the TCP connection and then said nothing left the row on Connecting, because cancelling a coroutine does not interrupt a blocked socket read. `disconnect()` also closes a socket that is still dialing.
- Writes are serialized (PPLI, chat and pings share the stream). `SO_KEEPALIVE` is on.
- Ping and pong frames are consumed by the connection: they do not count as received messages, are not parsed into contacts and are not relayed to the mesh.

**Fix, in the reconnect supervisor.** It collected the connection's `StateFlow`, and a collector is only handed a value that differs from the last one it saw. A dial that failed the same way twice (Failed, Connecting, Failed) faster than the collector came back around looked like no change, and `drop(1)` could swallow a first dial that had already failed. Either way the retries stopped until the app was opened. With real sockets that needs unlucky timing; a phone with no network, where a dial fails within a millisecond, is where it is most likely. Run against a dial that fails at once, the old loop made 0 or 1 attempts in ten minutes. The supervisor is now `superviseReconnect()`, a loop that reads the state afresh on each pass. It also starts its backoff over only after a connection has held for 10 s; before, a server that accepted and dropped at once was re-dialed as fast as the dials completed.

Cost on an idle link: one ping of about 230 bytes and its answer every 15 s. A busy link sends none once the server has answered the first.

**Tests.** `./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest`: 1042 tests, 0 failures (1019 on main). The new ones also pass with every CPU core kept busy.
- `TAKConnectionLivenessTest`, 17 tests against real sockets on loopback: the app's first event reaches the server before any ping; a busy stream is pinged until the server has answered once and not after; a quiet server that answers stays up across several drop windows; one that stops answering is reported Failed; one that sends the ping back counts as answering; another client's relayed ping does not; one that never answered is not dropped; a ten minute jump of the clock does not drop the link; a write blocked on a dead path does not stop the check; the ping exchange is not delivered as CoT; a failed send ends the connection; a closed stream reads Disconnected; a re-dial at the moment of failure is not lost; a stalled TLS handshake fails within the timeout; disconnect during a dial stays Disconnected and a later dial still runs; the ping and the frame probes.
- `ReconnectSupervisorTest`, 6 tests on virtual time: a dial that fails the same way every time keeps being retried on the 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30 s curve; a connection that has held resets the curve; a server that drops every connection at once is not dialed in a tight loop; a switched-off server is not dialed; a dial in flight is left alone; a connection brought back during the backoff is not dialed again.

**Checked in the running app.** Against a stand-in server on the development machine (reached with `adb reverse`) that answers pings like a TAK server, can be told to keep its sockets open and say nothing, and can be stopped.

Final build, on an emulator (Android 16), read from the server's log, the app's log and the status bar:

| Situation | What the app did |
|---|---|
| Connect | Its position report was the first frame. The first ping followed 15.1 s after the connect and was answered. |
| Idle link | A ping every 15 s, each answered. The received counter stayed at 0: pongs are not counted. |
| Server goes silent | Two pings went unanswered. The link was dropped 50.1 s after the last byte received (`Connection dropped: No response from server`) and re-dialed at once. |
| Server stays silent | Each new connection sent its position report, pinged after 15 and 30 s, and was dropped after 45 s. This is the known limit below. |
| Server answers again | The next connection got its pongs and stayed up. Green dot. |
| Server gone (every dial accepted and dropped at once) | Dials at 0, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 30 s, not a tight loop. Red dot. Connected on the next attempt after the server came back. |

Before, on a phone (Pixel Fold, Android 17, 0.44.0, the same connection code as main): after 180 s of the same silence the dot was still green, the send counter kept ticking and nothing had been received. The first commit of this branch was also run on that phone and dropped the link 45.2 s after the last byte; the final build has only been run on the emulator.

**Against a real server.** taky 0.10 (an open-source TAK server) on the development machine, final build on the emulator:
- taky registered the client under the app's own UID and callsign, taken from its position report. No second client appeared for the ping.
- Idle for over two minutes: no drop.
- taky paused (process stopped, sockets left open): the app dropped the link within 40 s of the pause with `No response from server` and re-dialed.
- taky resumed: the new connection stayed up.

How the other servers answer the ping was read in their source, not run: TAK Server and goatak send a `t-x-c-t-r` pong (TAK Server's with single-quoted attributes); OpenTAKServer's current master sends the ping back.

**Not verified.**
- The final build on a physical phone.
- TAK Server and OpenTAKServer themselves (see above).
- The TLS path on a phone. The liveness logic is shared with plain TCP, and the handshake timeout is covered by a unit test on the JVM's TLS stack, not Android's.
- Hours of Doze.

**Known limits.**
- A path that accepts the TCP connection and then answers nothing shows Connected for about 45 s on each retry when the server is plain TCP. With TLS the handshake fails instead. Showing "connected, nothing heard yet" differently belongs to #245.
- iOS has no ping either: engindearing-projects/OmniTAK-iOS#149.

title: fix(servers): one health projection for the top bar and the Servers screen (#209)
body:
Closes #209

**Root cause.** The top bar and the Servers screen each turned `ServerManager`'s per-server state into colours on their own, with different rules, so one set of states could read green on one and red on the other:

- With two or more enabled servers the bar's "N/M" count went green as soon as any server was up (`ATAKStatusBar`, `connected > 0`). "1/2" with the other server Failed was green on the bar and red on that server's row.
- The Servers row painted its Stop button `HostileRed` whenever the row was Connected or Connecting, so a healthy green row carried a red icon.
- The row's dot had a dim-green branch for the active server even when it was not connected, and the bar's per-server dots were two-state (green or red) while the rows told connected, connecting, failed and idle apart.

With a single enabled server the bar (`connState is Connected || connectedIds.isNotEmpty()`) and the row both come from the same `_serverStates` snapshot (`ServerManager.recomputeAggregate()`), so they cannot disagree for long. With one server the only red on a healthy row was that Stop icon.

**Fix.** One pure projection in `domain/ServerHealth.kt`, called by both surfaces.

- Per server, `ServerHealthProjection.project(enabled, state)`: CONNECTED, CONNECTING, FAILED, DISCONNECTED or DISABLED. Disabled wins over any stale state entry. The issue lists four values; I added DISCONNECTED for an enabled server with no live socket and nothing in flight (the operator pressed Stop, which removes its state entry, or the socket just dropped). It is not an error, so it gets a neutral grey dot, and it counts as "not connected" in the aggregate.
- Aggregate, `ServerHealthProjection.aggregate(...)`: every enabled server connected is GREEN, none connected (including none enabled) is RED, anything in between is AMBER. "None connected" is checked first, so a lone Failed or Connecting server stays red as before; amber is the mixed case that used to read green.
- Bar: `ATAKStatusBar` takes a `ServerHealthSummary` instead of `isConnected` + `serverConnectedFlags`. The single dot uses the aggregate colour. With more than one enabled server the "N/M" text uses the aggregate colour and each dot is that server's own health (green, amber, red, grey).
- Servers screen: the row dot and the Stop/Play state come from the same `project(...)`. The dim-green dot is gone (the left accent stripe already marks the active server). The Stop icon is now a neutral grey instead of red. Play keeps the accent colour.
- One colour mapping (`ui/components/ServerHealthColors.kt`) is used by both, so a state cannot be green on one screen and red on the other. The bar's red is now `HostileRed` (it was `0xFFE53935`, the rows used `0xFFF44336`).

Not in this PR: dead-socket detection. `TAKConnection` has `READ_TIMEOUT_MS = 0`, no keepalive, and a failed `send()` leaves the state Connected, so a half-open socket still reads CONNECTED here, on the bar and on the row alike. The issue's "no traffic for the keepalive window" amber needs that detection first, so it is left for a separate issue (dead TAK socket never detected).

**Tests.** `ServerHealthTest` (new, 19 tests):

- Per-server projection: every connection state, disabled wins over a stale `Connected` entry, a missing entry is DISCONNECTED.
- Aggregate: none/only disabled, lone server in each state, all up, up+failed (the #209 case), up+connecting, up+stopped, none up, disabled ignored, plus an exhaustive check over every combination of up to three servers (GREEN needs all up, AMBER needs some but not all, RED means none, and a Failed server never leaves the bar green).
- `summarize`: counts and order, stale entries for unlisted servers ignored, and the bar and the rows cannot disagree for the same state (all state pairs for two servers).
- Against the real `ServerManager` (FakeServerStore + TestScope, same pattern as `ServerManagerToggleTest`): the projection follows toggle on/off, and Stop on a row leaves the enabled server DISCONNECTED with a red bar.

`./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest --max-workers=2 -Dorg.gradle.jvmargs="-Xmx2560m -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8" -Dkotlin.daemon.jvm.options=-Xmx1536m`

Result: 874 tests (855 before, 19 new), 0 failures, 9 skipped (pre-existing, in `DeepLinkEnrollTest` and `GeoTIFFParserTest`).

**Verification still needed.** I did not run the app, so none of the colours are observed on a device. With two enabled servers (for example one reachable and one with a wrong port):

- The bar shows amber "1/2" with a green dot and a second dot that alternates red (Failed) and amber (Connecting) as that server retries. The failing row's dot does the same, and the connected row has a green dot with a grey Stop icon.
- Tap Stop on the connected row: its dot goes grey, the bar goes red "0/2", Play appears.
- Turn the second server off with its switch: the bar goes back to a single-server look based on the remaining one (green when connected) and the off row is dim grey.
- Single server: green dot on the bar and on the row with a grey Stop icon while connected; red on the bar while Connecting (as before this change).
- Compare the dot colours on the bar and the rows side by side once, since the bar's red shade moved slightly.
