title: Fix: Recognize Samsung's automatic battery protection on One UI 8
body:
## What changed

On One UI 8, Samsung turns on Maximum battery protection by itself when a phone or tablet stays plugged in for long periods. Amply didn't recognize that state, so the dashboard showed "Policy not verified" with "Unrecognized value: protect_battery=2", and "Charge to 100% once" wasn't available.

Amply now shows it as the protection limit it is (for example "80% limit"), notes that the system turned it on automatically, and allows a one-time full charge from it. Afterwards Amply restores the same limit as a regular Maximum setting.

## Technical Context

- Device Care writes `protect_battery=2` for this mode (its long-term charging feature, `longtermcharge/LtcWorker`). On a Tab A9+ (One UI 8.0) Samsung's own screen showed Maximum 80 % and the battery held at 80 %.
- The adapter reads 2 as `FixedLimit(threshold)` and flags the observation `systemManaged`. Amply never writes 2, so the privileged write allowlist stays `{0,1,3}`; a restore writes 1.
- An external write of 1 leaves Samsung's long-term-charging bookkeeping keys untouched. Whether Samsung still restores its saved previous mode when long-term charging ends and it finds 1 is unverified; the worst case is the device staying on Maximum. Details are in the qualification ledger.
- `ChargeObservation.Verified` gains an optional `systemManaged` flag (default false); every existing comparison uses `.policy`, so other adapters are unaffected.

title: Fix: Show the real current and charge power on some Samsung phones
body:
## What changed

Some Samsung phones report the battery current in milliamps instead of microamps, so Amply showed "0 mA" and "0.0 W" while charging. Amply now works out which unit a Samsung device uses and shows the real current and charge power. It learns this the first time Amply reads the battery for about a minute while the phone is unplugged with the screen on, and remembers it until the next system update.

Samsung phones that already report correctly are left alone.

Refs #92

## Technical Context

- Not every Samsung reports milliamps. A Galaxy S20 FE on One UI 4.1 reports them plugged and unplugged, while a Galaxy Tab A9+ on One UI 8.0 reports microamps, so a manufacturer-only rule would multiply correct readings by 1000.
- Milliamp evidence is only taken unplugged with the screen on (three or more readings over 60 s, each under 10,000). A charge-limit hold draws next to nothing and only exists while plugged, which is what sank the earlier data-driven designs recorded in the qualification ledger. Any reading of 20,000 or more proves microamps and wins permanently.
- Only the current is rescaled; the charge counter is already correct on these devices. The existing MagicOS whole-readout correction takes precedence, so nothing is scaled twice.
- The verdict is stored per ROM build and loaded in the background. Until it loads, the Samsung current reads as "Not reported" rather than an uncorrected value, because the reader also runs on the main thread and must not block.
- Worth a close look: the persistence path in `BatteryUnitCalibration` (single write in flight, retry on failure, follow-up write when a stronger verdict lands mid-write). Charge history recorded before this fix keeps its old values.

title: General: Fix an intermittently failing charge-time test
body:
## What changed

No user-facing behavior change. Fixes an intermittent timeout in `ChargeTimeModelSourceTest > a newly finished session does re-fold the history` (seen in run 35850592967).

## Technical Context

- Root cause: the test helper inserted an already-finished session row, then its samples one by one. The model source re-folds only when the finished-session id list changes. A fold landing between the row and its samples saw the new session with no observations, and the later sample inserts didn't change the ids, so the 3-session model never arrived.
- The helper now inserts the row and its samples in one Room transaction. That matches production, where the recorder writes samples to an open session and only then seals it.
- Forcing a 500 ms gap between the row and its samples makes the old helper fail every time, while the transactional helper passes.

title: Fix: Stop showing a charge session that has already finished
body:
## What changed

A temporary "charge once to 100%" session could finish while the notification kept saying it was still running. Three further problems could leave the app unable to manage charging after a session or a recovery: a slow Shizuku connection could silently stop the background monitor for as long as the app kept running, a failed recovery could crash the app, and a failed widget refresh could shut the service down right after it had decided to keep going. All four are fixed.

## Technical Context

- `TimeoutCancellationException` is a `CancellationException`, and `DispatchCoordinator` deliberately ends a consumer coroutine when a handler throws one, so a Shizuku bind timeout escaping `applyLocked` killed battery evaluation for the life of the service. Timeouts are now classified as failed writes at both the write and post-write sites.
- `SurfaceUpdater.updateNow` propagates widget enqueue failures by design, so any call preceding a terminal teardown step can skip it. Eight of the nine sites in `ChargeSessionService` now carry the guard; the ninth is deliberate, because its terminal call already ran and the dispatch coordinator contains the throw.
- The recovery job ran on a supervisor scope with no exception handler, so a hook failure reached the thread's default handler. It now runs through `RecoveryJobFlow`, which logs, warns and still runs the terminal continuation, and whose last resort is `stopForeground` plus `stopSelf` rather than `stopMonitoring`, which needs dispatch exclusivity that has just failed.
- Guarding the two post-commit pushes also closes a pre-existing crash path, since the settings observer's own `launch` has no handler and a widget failure reached from a native settings change was uncaught.
- Worth close review: the catch ordering in all three new pairs, where the subtype must precede the supertype, and `ChargingRepositoryPostWriteTest`'s fault injection, which depends on the Pixel adapter's unguarded `registerReceiver` sitting inside the post-write `try`.

title: Fix: Correct wrong battery power and current readings on HONOR
body:
## What changed

On HONOR phones running MagicOS, Amply's battery figures were wrong by a factor of a thousand. The charge counter showed "7 mAh" instead of about 7000, charging power read "0.0 W" while the phone was fast charging, and the current reading showed a few mA (or zero) no matter what the phone was actually doing. The phone reports these values in different units than Android specifies, and Amply took them at face value.

Amply now recognises MagicOS and corrects both readings, but only when that phone's numbers actually show the problem, so a HONOR build that reports correctly is left alone. No other manufacturer's phone is affected in any way.

Reported by a contributor on a Magic8 Pro who also confirmed it with a screenshot.

## Technical Context

- The ROM reports `BATTERY_PROPERTY_CURRENT_NOW` and `BATTERY_PROPERTY_CHARGE_COUNTER` in milli-units where `BatteryManager` documents micro-units. Confirmed rather than inferred: the counter read `6978` for a 7100 mAh cell (Amply rendered `round(6978/1000)` = "7 mAh", matching the reporter's own `dumpsys`), and current read 0 mA while discharging with the screen on, since a real ~300 mA arrives as `300`.
- Correction requires **both** a ROM match (system feature, either of two, no `<queries>` or permission needed) **and** the anomaly in the reading: implied full-charge capacity `counter × 100 / percent` below 100 mAh. That normalizes out the charge level and separates a correct phone (≥ ~1_000_000 µAh at any level) from a milli-reporting one (single-digit thousands) by an order of magnitude either side.
- **Two purely data-driven designs were built and rejected first, and the second is the one worth reviewing.** Corroborating the counter anomaly against an implausibly small charging current fails because a device at a charge-limit hold reports exactly that signature, and this app creates holds deliberately: `StatsLimitHitDetector` uses `abs(current) < 50_000 µA` while `CHARGING` to *recognise* a hold. A healthy phone holding at 80% with a broken charge counter would have latched and had its readings multiplied by a thousand, which at ~50 mA computes to ~200 W, under `StatsPowerCalculator`'s 250 W ceiling and so recorded as a credible lie rather than a visible error. `BatteryReadoutFactoryTest` pins that case.
- Generalising "all MagicOS" from one device is deliberate and is a much cheaper bet than the equivalent for charge control: the failure mode is a wrong battery figure, not a false claim that a battery is protected. The gate can only ever affect a ROM on the list.
- `BatteryReader` gains a constructor dependency, which is why five unrelated test files are touched. `max_charging_*` is deliberately not rescaled (separate intent extras, never observed populated on the affected device), and history recorded before this fix keeps its old values, so a chart spanning the upgrade shows a step on affected devices only.

Refs #66

title: Fix: Open the right battery screen on unsupported devices
body:
## What changed

On a phone Amply has no charge-protection support for, the "Open battery settings" button opened the system Battery saver screen. That screen has no charge-protection toggle in it, so the button led nowhere useful on exactly the devices that needed it most. It now opens the battery-usage screen, which on most manufacturer skins is where the built-in charging-protection option actually lives, and only falls back to Battery saver when a phone has no battery-usage screen at all.

This was reported on a HONOR phone but applied to every brand Amply carries no support for, including Motorola, Nothing, Sony, Fairphone, Vivo and Tecno. The same button in the "Help add support" wizard is fixed by the same change.

Also fixes a crash: if opening the battery screen failed, the retry could throw and take the action down with it.

The remaining two commits change no behavior. One corrects a wrong explanation in the code about how charging-power readings can be misreported, and pins the current behavior in a test. The other records a contributor's hardware measurements in the device-qualification ledger.

## Technical Context

- Root cause: `ChargingRepository.nativeSettingsIntent()` returned null when `AdapterRegistry` matched no adapter, and its single caller substituted `ACTION_BATTERY_SAVER_SETTINGS` outright. `ACTION_POWER_USAGE_SUMMARY` was therefore never attempted, despite all four lab adapters preferring it and the manifest already declaring its `<queries>` visibility. Same user-visible symptom the ledger records for LineageOS, reached by a different path (that one fell through to the Pixel component intent; this one had no adapter object to ask at all).
- The chain moved to `OemChargingShortcuts.genericBatterySettings` so the null path and `DisabledLabAdapter` share one implementation instead of a sixth copy, and the repository's return type is now non-null so no caller can reintroduce its own fallback. The four OEM adapters keep their private copies deliberately: converting them would couple qualified per-device navigation to whatever "generic" comes to mean later.
- The crash was pre-existing for unmapped devices: on a launch failure the handler retried the *same* Battery Saver intent outside `runCatching`, so when that intent was the one that failed, the second throw escaped. It now skips a fallback that would repeat the failed action, and guards and logs both attempts. Worth a close look, since it is the one place this PR changes control flow rather than intent selection.
- `POWER_USAGE_SUMMARY` is verified to resolve only under Robolectric here. Whether it resolves on MagicOS 10 specifically is unconfirmed, so this is not proven to change what the original reporter sees. The change is correct for unmapped devices generally either way.
- The `StatsPowerCalculator` commit deliberately does **not** fix the underlying defect. A firmware reporting `CURRENT_NOW` in mA where Android documents µA makes readings 1000× too small, which the plausibility cap cannot catch, but no lower bound can separate that from a genuine end-of-charge trickle either. The test states why not to add one; the real fix needs charge-level context this function does not have.

Refs #66

title: Fix: Reconnect gesture stopped working after a mistimed replug
body:
## What changed

The reconnect gesture could get stuck. If you unplugged and replugged slightly outside the 2–10 second window, the gesture silently lost its arming — and because a reconnect window only opens while the gesture is armed, every further attempt did nothing. It stayed dead until the charge limit settled back in on its own, which is why repeated tries felt like the feature was broken. Turning on "any charge level" hid the problem, so that looked like the only way to make the gesture work at all.

A mistimed attempt now keeps the arming, so retrying works.

Two further changes:

- Applying a charge policy from the dashboard now takes the same path as the widget's buttons, which adds the safety checks the dashboard was missing.
- The gesture no longer stays armed once the battery moves outside the 75–90% range, so a charge limit removed in system settings can no longer leave it armed while the battery keeps charging.

## Technical Context

**Root cause.** `QuickFullChargeGesture` latched the arming basis but discarded it on every replug edge and re-derived it from the instantaneous reading. A physically replugged phone at 80% reports `BATTERY_STATUS_CHARGING` while it tops back up, so a limit-hold basis can never be re-derived at that instant. The unplug edge only opens a reconnect window when a basis is latched, which is what produced the dead-gesture state. The any-level basis needs only `plugged && PROTECTIVE` — both true at that same tick — which is why enabling it masked the bug.

**Why it was never caught.** `QuickFullChargeGestureTest` fed a settled-hold reading (`NOT_CHARGING` + charging state 4) as the *replug* tick, which is physically impossible. The project's `dumpsys battery unplug` recipe freezes reported state and reproduces the same impossible reading, so the defect was invisible to both unit tests and simulated device runs, and surfaced only with a real cable.

**Approach.** `armedBy` + `disconnectedAtMillis` are replaced by a sealed `State` (`Idle` / `Armed(basis)` / `AwaitingReconnect(basis, sinceMillis)`). Every prior transition is preserved; the only behavioural change is that a replug shorter than `minReconnectMillis` returns to `Armed` with the carried basis instead of re-deriving. No existing test assertion changed.

**Deliberate non-bound.** The carried basis intentionally holds no timestamp. A bounded variant — expiring it 10 s after the original unplug — was considered and rejected: a human retry after a failed attempt is frequently slower than 10 s, so that bound would re-break the reported bug for exactly the people who hit it. The test `a retry long after the original unplug still triggers` pins this so a future change cannot quietly reintroduce it.

**Out-of-band retirement.** A `percent` outside 75–90 now retires a `LIMIT_HOLD` basis. This addresses a **pre-existing** gap, not this bug — the steady-plugged branch has never dropped a latched basis, so a limit removed in system settings left the gesture armed as the battery climbed. It deliberately does not touch an any-level basis (percent-independent by design) and ignores `percent < 0`, so a single failed sticky-broadcast read cannot disarm a healthy gesture. It runs before the plug edges, so it also cancels an already-open window.

**Dashboard policy path.** `DashboardViewModel.applyPolicy` now sends `ACTION_SET_PERSISTENT_POLICY` instead of calling `repository.applyPersistent` directly. Beyond resetting the gesture engine, this gains the `canApply` refusal guard, a recovery target persisted before the write, settings-observer suppression, `reapplyPersistent`'s forced re-write, and failure surfacing. `ChargeSessionManager` became unused in the ViewModel and was dropped from its constructor.

**Review guidance.** The state-machine rewrite is the risk surface. Worth checking transition equivalence against the previous `armedBy`/`disconnectedAtMillis` pair — in particular the any-level revocation guard (`disconnectedAtMillis == null` became `state !is AwaitingReconnect`) and the `statusOutput` mapping.

**Verification.** On a Pixel 8 holding at its 80% limit: after a rejected sub-2 s blip the notification stays on the armed copy (the previous build fell back to the idle copy), the retry then starts a session, and disconnecting restores the limit. Forcing level 95 confirmed the out-of-band retirement, and it re-armed on reset. Unit suite: 1574 tests green across both flavours.

title: Fix: Reconnect gesture did nothing unless Amply set the limit
body:
## What changed

**The reconnect gesture now actually fires.** Previously it only armed if the protective charge limit had been applied *through Amply itself*. If the limit was already set on the phone — configured in system settings, left over from an earlier install, or predating an app update that reset stored preferences — the gesture silently did nothing: the ongoing notification sat on its idle text forever and a quick unplug/replug never started a full charge. Amply now also trusts the phone's live charging state, so a limit it didn't set itself still arms the gesture.

**The gesture's options moved into a new "Charging" screen in Settings.** The dashboard card no longer carries a settings shortcut — it keeps just its on/off switch. The new screen holds both the master switch and the "Any charge level" option, and it respects the same availability rules as the dashboard card, so the gesture can't be switched on where the card correctly forbids it.

**The ongoing notification now tells you the condition it will fire under.** It reads "Ready at your 80% limit…" or "Ready at any charge level…" depending on the "Any charge level" setting, and switches to a short "Reconnect now: replug within 10 seconds…" while the replug window is open. Previously all of these states shared one line of text.

## Technical Context

**Root cause.** The any-level arming basis gated on the stored record of persistent policy writes, which is empty until Amply performs its first write. On an affected device that record is absent while the limit genuinely is active, so the basis never armed. Confirmed on-device: the stored record held no policy entry, while settings readback reported a verified 80% limit and the battery broadcast reported the corresponding charging-policy hardware state.

**Why the evidence is tri-state.** The obvious fix — OR the hardware signal into the existing boolean — does not work. The charging-policy extra is only reported while external power is present, so the unplug tick reports nothing, and the state machine evaluates its revocation rule *before* it records the powered→unpowered edge. A boolean would therefore revoke the basis on the very tick that should open the reconnect window. Evidence is now `PROTECTIVE` / `UNRESTRICTED` / `UNKNOWN`: only an explicit opt-out or conclusive unrestricted evidence revokes, while `UNKNOWN` is tolerated on an unplugged tick or inside an open window. A *plugged* tick that goes inconclusive does revoke — powered, the evidence is available, so an inconclusive reading means the configuration is no longer known to be protective; it simply re-arms on the next protective tick. The `disconnectedAtMillis == null` guard in that condition is load-bearing: without it, a replug tick whose hardware has not yet re-reported its hold would destroy its own trigger.

**Protection is `!allowsFullCharge`, not `!= Unrestricted`** — `PauseAtFull` and a 100% fixed limit both reach full charge and must not arm a gesture whose purpose is to lift a cap.

**Notification percentage sourcing.** The named percentage comes only from a verified observation, never from the write journal: the journal records what Amply last wrote, not what is configured now, so a limit removed in system settings would otherwise keep being claimed. The stored protective baseline is deliberately not a source either — it defaults to 80% with no history and retains a stale value after an unrestricted write. Consequence: an unverified state falls back to generic wording rather than naming a number.

**Armed copy states the firing condition, not the latched basis.** At the limit, the limit-hold basis wins the latch even when the any-level option is on and qualifying, so reporting the latched basis understated a gesture that will in fact fire at any level. The copy now derives from the option plus current protective evidence.

**Adapter resolution** stays inside the gesture branch, behind the session early-return and the cheap enabled check — resolving device info walks package/provider lookups, and hoisting it would newly charge active sessions, disabled gestures and watcher-only ticks for it under the command mutex. Net cost is unchanged.

**Known residual (deliberate).** With "Any charge level" on, inconclusive hardware evidence plus a stale protective journal still arms even if charging was since set unrestricted outside Amply. Session start refuses whenever the current policy is verifiable, so this only applies without Shizuku, and it is pre-existing behaviour. Failing closed would reverse the documented rule that a stale last-request must never block a session, and would disable the gesture entirely for users without Shizuku.

**Review guidance.** The state-machine change is the risk surface; the pure engine and its evidence resolver are covered by JVM tests, including regressions for the unplug-tick and open-window cases. The rest is UI wiring and copy. The system Back grouping was fixed, not just renamed, so both back paths from the new screen land on Settings.

## Verification

- 739 unit tests, lint (both flavors, beta + release), and both flavor debug assembles pass.
- Device-verified end to end on a Pixel 9 Pro (Android 16) against the actual broken state — the unplug/replug now produces a trigger and starts a session, and both notification variants were confirmed on the same build. Battery-protection state was restored and verified afterwards.
- The Play Store screenshot showing the old gesture screen was regenerated.

title: Stats: Live current-session card, chart axes, session timestamps, empty-session fix
body:
## What changed

Four battery-statistics improvements, requested together:

1. **Session detail now shows the date/time.** The charge-session detail screen adds absolute **Started** / **Ended** rows, so a session is no longer context-free.
2. **The charge curve has axis context.** Each series in the legend now shows its **min→max value with unit** (e.g. `Level 42→100%`, `Power 1.5→25.0 W`, `Temperature 30.0→34.0 °C`), and an **elapsed-time x axis** is drawn beneath the plot.
3. **A live "Charging now" card on the dashboard.** While the device is plugged in (and statistics recording is on), a card appears **directly under the battery hero** showing the current charge session at a glance — `start% → now%`, how long it's been charging, live power/temperature, and a compact live curve. Tapping it opens the statistics screen. When the device isn't charging, the dashboard looks as it did before (the compact stats card stays in its usual position lower down).
4. **Fixed: toggling "Record statistics" no longer creates an empty session.** Flipping the recording toggle on then off while plugged in used to leave a bogus 0-minute charge session in the history. A session that captured nothing is now discarded instead of saved.

## Technical Context

**Empty-session fix.** The root cause: enabling capture while already plugged opens a session on the immediate monitor tick, and the following disable seals it with `end == start`. `StatsSessionEngine.isDiscardable()` decides on the sealed **outcome** — zero elapsed **and** no level gain **and** ≤1 sample — rather than sample count alone, so a genuine sub-cadence plug that recorded real time or a charge delta is retained. The sticky limit/override flags are deliberately **not** a keep-reason: a single instantaneous sample that merely observed an OEM hold, with no elapsed time or curve, is still the empty artifact, so it's dropped even when the toggle happens at a limit. Applied in both `sealCurrent` and dangling-session recovery.

**Live card data sources.** "Now" telemetry (level / power / temperature) comes from the shared 3-second `BatteryReadout` — the same source the hero uses — so the two adjacent cards never disagree, rather than the ~30-second-stale recorder row. Room supplies only the session start, the `partial` flag, and a **bounded** recent-sample curve (an open session can last days at an OEM limit, so the curve query is windowed + decimated, not an unbounded reload per sample). Elapsed time is derived from `SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()` — monotonic, immune to wall-clock/NTP changes, and the same clock the curve uses.

**Open-session flow safety.** The new reactive open-session query is filtered to the **current boot** (so a pre-reboot dangling row can't briefly flash "Charging now" before startup repair seals it) and ordered by `id` (monotonic autoincrement; elapsed-realtime resets across a reboot). `distinctUntilChangedBy(id)` keeps the curve subscription stable across per-tick row updates. All new reads are read-only Room flows; the recorder keeps sole write ownership and gains only the two discard branches.

**Chart correctness.** X-axis tick labels are formatted from the chart's own drawable x-range, so a label can never disagree with the plotted endpoints. The legend is a `FlowRow` (three range chips wrap instead of overflowing on narrow screens); sub-minute spans render seconds; duplicate ticks collapse. A `chartHeight` parameter keeps the live card's chart compact.

**Scope.** No schema change (no Room migration). No charge-control, Shizuku/WSS, AIDL, or capability-gate surface is touched — this is stats UI + read-side plumbing only.

## Testing

- `testFossDebugUnitTest` + `testGplayDebugUnitTest`: **443 tests pass**.
- `assembleFossDebug` + `assembleGplayDebug`, and `lintVital` (both flavors, beta + release): pass, no warnings.
- New/extended tests: `isDiscardable` boundary (drops the artifact, retains a real short session, drops-at-OEM-hold, retains a real hold that accrued time); DAO (targeted delete + cascade, current-boot open-session flow, id-ordering, cross-boot exclusion, bounded recent-sample window); a Robolectric Compose test for the live-vs-unplugged card gating; and a deterministic date/axis formatter test.
- Reviewed by Codex (cross-vendor) + a second reviewer; all findings integrated (outcome-based discard predicate, monotonic elapsed, current-boot filter, chart edge cases).

**On-device verification is still recommended** before release — the live card, the plugged-gate, and the discard-at-seal path have unit + Robolectric coverage but haven't had a hardware smoke pass.

title: Fix: UpdateManager build verification
body: Now update manager checks `SHA256 hash` of app's signature before proceeding with installation. This PR should close #6

title: fix(server): 🐛 ignore Kubernetes service-link variables in config warnings
body:
## The story

Rolling out #138 to production, the new pod logged six warnings at boot:

```
Unknown setting QUIRE_SERVER_PORT_80_TCP is ignored; check the spelling against docs/configuration.md
Unknown setting QUIRE_SERVER_PORT_80_TCP_ADDR is ignored; ...
Unknown setting QUIRE_SERVER_PORT_80_TCP_PORT is ignored; ...
Unknown setting QUIRE_SERVER_PORT_80_TCP_PROTO is ignored; ...
Unknown setting QUIRE_SERVER_SERVICE_HOST is ignored; ...
Unknown setting QUIRE_SERVER_SERVICE_PORT is ignored; ...
```

Nobody set these. Kubernetes gives every pod a set of variables describing each Service in its namespace, named after the Service, and ours is called `quire-server`. They share the settings prefix, so the typo check from #104 reports them, and `GET /health` repeats them as warnings. An operator reading the health output would go hunting for typos that are not there. None of them changes a setting: the bare `QUIRE_SERVER_PORT` form was already excluded as compose-only, and no setting is named like the others.

## What changes in practice

The unknown-variable scan skips names that match the Kubernetes pattern for a Service called `quire-server`: `…_SERVICE_HOST`, `…_SERVICE_PORT` (with or without a port name), and `…_PORT_<number>_<TCP|UDP|SCTP>` with its `_ADDR`, `_PORT` and `_PROTO` variants. The match is exact, so a real typo such as `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_MODLE`, or a near miss like `QUIRE_SERVER_SERVICE_HOSTNAME`, is still flagged. `docs/configuration.md` says so where it lists the warnings.

## What does not change

Every other warning, and the check itself for any other name. Production keeps logging the six lines until the next server rollout.

## How it was checked

- A new test with all six names from the production log (plus a named-port variant) fails before the change and passes after it, with a typo and a near miss still reported.
- Full server suite: 903 passed. ruff 0.16.8 is clean, and the docs-drift test passes.

In short: the boot check stops reporting Kubernetes' own variables as the operator's typos.

title: fix(server): 🐛 get AI insights working again on Ollama's cloud models
body:
## The story

Rolling out the status page moved the production server from an image built in May straight to today's, and AI insights stopped working. Every request came back 502 with "The model gpt-oss:120b-cloud may be too small for structured JSON output".

The cause is #114, from 22 September. It moved the insight schema out of the prompt and into `response_format: json_schema`, trusting that a provider without schema support would refuse with a 4xx and trigger the fallback. Ollama's cloud models answer 200 and ignore the schema, and on that server every chat model is a cloud model. With the schema gone from the prompt, the model invents a shape of its own: `author` as an object, comparison items with their own keys. The retry fails the same way, twice, every time.

A probe on the cluster, same model, asking for a made-up shape it cannot guess:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| Schema only in `response_format` (what the server sends today) | wrong shape, 2 of 2 |
| Ollama's own `format` parameter | wrong shape |
| Schema in the prompt, `json_object` (before #114) | right shape |
| Schema in both | right shape, 3 of 3 |

## What changes in practice

- **A shape the schema forbids now counts as proof.** When a `json_schema` answer leaves out a required key or adds one the schema forbids, the provider ignored the schema, because any runtime that enforces it rules both out. On that proof the retry spells the schema out in the prompt, still in `json_schema` mode, and so does every later call in that process. The switch is logged once, as `ai.client.schema_in_prompt model=... reason=provider_ignored_json_schema`.
- **Wrong values and cut-off answers do not count.** They can slip past enforcement, the retry's error message handles them, and the schema written out is about 7,000 characters: sending it every time would more than double each prompt, which a CPU-only model like the one in #102 pays for in seconds.
- **On a cloud model the cost is one failed attempt per server start,** spent inside the retry the client already makes, so no insight fails because of it.
- **The parse-error hint stops going in a circle.** It no longer recommends gpt-oss:120b-cloud to someone running gpt-oss:120b-cloud. For that model it points at the server log instead.

## What does not change

Providers that do enforce the schema (local Ollama, llama.cpp, OpenAI) never trip the switch and keep #114's short prompt. The 4xx fallback is unchanged. It now also sets the new flag, since it always sent the schema in the prompt.

## How it was checked

- 5 new tests: an ignored schema is spelled out on the retry, later calls keep it, a wrong value and a cut-off answer keep the prompt short, and the hint. The two behaviour tests failed before the fix.
- I broke the fix three ways (wrong values counted as proof, cut-off answers counted, the switch forgotten between calls), and a test failed each time.
- The full server suite passes, 886 tests, and ruff 0.16.8 is clean.
- I ran the patched client inside the production pod, against the real model with the real system prompt and payload, on three books from the failing logs. The first failed exactly as in the logs, switched, and succeeded on the retry. The next two succeeded on the first request.

In short: when a provider says yes to a schema and then ignores it, the server notices from the answer and spells the schema out, instead of failing every insight.

title: fix(android): 🐛 covers for imported books, tappable option names, no 16 KB warning, and a working scanner
body:
The reader fixes in #128 left three follow-ups on the list: books imported from a file never got a cover, tapping a font's name in reader settings did nothing, and new phones showed a system warning that Quire "isn't 16 KB compatible". Checking those turned up four more, including one that broke the barcode scanner outright. Each is its own commit.

## What changes for a reader

**Imported books show their cover.** A book imported from a file (in-app Import, or "Open with Quire" from a file manager) only ever showed its initials, because `SideloadImporter` never extracted the cover. It now finds the cover image the EPUB's OPF declares (EPUB 3 `cover-image`, or EPUB 2 `<meta name="cover">`; a `<guide>` cover points at an XHTML page, not a picture, so it is ignored) and writes it next to the book as `<uuid>.cover`, the same convention catalog downloads use. A cover up to 512 KB and 1800 px passes through untouched; a bigger one is scaled to 900 px on its long edge. Books imported before this change get their covers once, on the first start after the update (`sideload.cover_backfill_done` marks it done), and only rows without a cover are touched.

**Deleting a book deletes its cover file.** `DocumentRepository.delete` removed the EPUB but left the cover behind, so every deleted book leaked an image in app storage.

**Tapping a font or theme's name selects it.** The reader's font and theme lists and the app theme and font lists in Settings only reacted to the small radio circle. A new `RadioOptionRow` makes the whole row the tap target, with the radio-button role for TalkBack, and each list is a `selectableGroup`.

**No more "isn't 16 KB compatible" dialog.** On a phone with 16 KB memory pages, such as the Pixel 10 image on Android 17, every launch and every "Open with Quire" import put up a system dialog and ran the app in compatibility mode. The culprit was CameraX 1.3.4's native library (4 KB aligned); the 1.3 line never shipped an aligned build. CameraX moves to 1.4.0, the first stable aligned release and the smallest step (1.4.1 adds a second native library). The other native library, Compose's `graphics-path`, was already aligned. The APK grows by 66 KB. Everything new is Apache-2.0 from Google Maven; no ML Kit or Play services enters the build, so the F-Droid recipe is unaffected, and `aboutlibraries.json` is regenerated for the drift check.

**Scanning a barcode finds the book again.** Every scan ended in "No book found": Open Library now answers 404 to every query on `/api/books`, the endpoint the scanner used. `/api/books.json` returns the same record. (The server's edition-language lookup had the same broken URL and was fixed in #129.)

**A full library no longer flashes "Your shelf is empty." on start.** The library rows started as an empty list until Room answered, so for a moment on every start the screen drew the empty shelf, plus the restore button for a connected account, over a library that has books. The rows are now null until Room first answers, and the screen draws nothing for those few milliseconds.

**Offline imports stop logging a stack trace.** In offline-only mode (and for an OPDS-only account) every import started a library upload pass that failed with "baseUrl not configured" and logged a full stack trace per unsynced book. The pass now returns at once when there is no server; the rows stay unsynced, so connecting a server later uploads them.

## Also in here

- **The flaky `LibraryViewModelTest > canRestore is false when connected but library non-empty` is fixed.** The race was in the test: with an unconfined Main dispatcher, the `canRestore` update ran on Room's thread, so the assertion could read a stale value before it landed (2 failures in 5,000 runs). The class now uses a `StandardTestDispatcher`, like `SettingsViewModelTest`; 0 failures in 5,000 runs.
- **`LibraryInsightsViewModelTest` waits up to 30 s instead of 5 s.** It talks to a real MockWebServer, and the first network test in a JVM timed out at 5.011 s on a loaded machine while still loading OkHttp. The bound only exists to catch a hang; a passing run settles in milliseconds.
- **The AboutLibraries drift check no longer reuses a cached dependency list.** This PR's first CI run failed that check although the committed `aboutlibraries.json` was right: `collectDependencies` and `exportLibraryDefinitions` came `FROM-CACHE`, because the plugin's task inputs don't capture resolved versions, so CI compared the file against main's pre-bump graph. Both tasks now never cache and never count as up to date (they run only on demand, in seconds), so the check sees the real graph after any dependency bump.
- **`scripts/dgradle` keeps Robolectric's downloads** in a `quire-m2-cache` volume, so a Docker test run no longer re-downloads the android-all jars (and fails on a network blip).

## How it was checked

- `./gradlew test lint :app:assembleDebug` passes locally, with every unit test green.
- New tests: the OPF cover locator and cover writer, the backfill (it runs once and leaves catalog books alone), cover deletion, the tappable row (Robolectric), the `/api/books.json` path, the loading state not reading as an empty shelf, the restore prompt never turning on while a non-empty library loads, and the uploader doing nothing without a server.
- On the 16 KB Pixel 10 emulator, against an `origin/main` build for contrast:
  - an EPUB imported on `main` showed initials; after upgrading to this branch its cover appeared on first launch, and a new import showed its cover straight away;
  - deleting a book removed both its `.epub` and `.cover`;
  - tapping "Open dyslexic" and "Sepia" by name moved the selection and re-rendered the text;
  - `main` showed the 16 KB dialog with `pageSizeCompat=4`; this branch showed none on fresh install, cold start or "Open with Quire", with `pageSizeCompat=0`, and the camera preview still decodes barcodes;
  - ISBN 9780141439518 found "Pride and Prejudice" by Jane Austen; `main` said "No book found".

Nothing changes on a phone until this ships in a release; the cover backfill then runs once on the first start.

title: fix(server): 🐛 accept the log level in any case, and repair two Open Library lookups
body:
Three small server problems: two the configuration guide (#125) made visible, one Open Library change.

**`QUIRE_SERVER_LOG_LEVEL=info` stopped the server at boot.** The value went straight to `logging.basicConfig`, which only knows the capitalised names, so a lower-case `info` (or an empty line) crashed startup with `ValueError: Unknown level` and Docker restarted the container in a loop. The setting is now typed as the five level names and a validator upper-cases and trims the value first:

- `info`, ` Debug ` and `WARNING` all work.
- An empty value means `INFO`, the default, instead of a crash.
- Any other word, such as `verbose`, still stops the server, but with pydantic's `validation error for Settings` that names `log_level` and lists the accepted values.

**Profile discovery's Open Library outages never showed on `/ai/v1/health`.** Since #127 wired profile discovery, its author-bibliography lookups recorded their health under `openlibrary_bibliography`. The health endpoint only lists the configured sources (`wikipedia`, `openlibrary`), so a discovery-time Open Library outage was recorded somewhere nobody could see it. The lookups now record under `openlibrary`; the cache rows keep their own `openlibrary_bibliography` names, so existing cached bibliographies stay valid.

**The edition-language lookup found nothing for any book.** Open Library now answers 404 to every query on `/api/books`, which `lookup_book_language` used to learn a scanned edition's language for the insight cards. So every lookup came back empty, and since a non-200 is deliberately not cached, it retried and failed again each time. `/api/books.json` serves the same response, so the lookup moves there; the test now pins the path. (The Android scanner had the same broken URL; that fix goes in the Android follow-ups PR.)

The guide's `LOG_LEVEL` entry and its "empty values" table now describe the new behaviour.

**Tests:** parametrised settings tests for case, whitespace and empty values plus a rejected word; two retrieval tests (the first tests `author_bibliography` has had) pinning that success and a 503 both land on the `openlibrary` health row. Full suite passes locally in all three modes: full 777 passed, sync_only 641 passed / 136 skipped, ai_only 675 passed / 102 skipped. Ruff clean.

Nothing changes for a deployment until the new server image is pulled; a capitalised log level behaves exactly as before.

title: fix(android): 🐛 make reader fonts, Gutenberg chapters and book metadata work as intended
fix(server): 🐛 offer books by the reader's top authors in the Reader Profile
body:
## Why

The Reader Profile has three kinds of suggestions. One of them, "more from authors you've finished", has never appeared on a self-hosted server. The README and `docs/architecture.md` both describe it: on refresh, the server asks Open Library for the works of the reader's top five authors, and the model picks the ones the reader doesn't own. The code for that step exists and is complete. But `create_app` never gave the AI service the retriever it needs, so the step quietly returned nothing, and every profile came back with an empty discovery list.

## What changes

- **`create_app` hands the profile path the same retriever it already uses for insight cards:** the same timeout (`QUIRE_SERVER_AI_RETRIEVAL_TIMEOUT_S`) and the same health reporting.
- **Discovery follows `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_SOURCES`, as card retrieval does.** An operator who drops `openlibrary` to keep the server off that site now keeps the profile off it too. Without this, wiring the retriever would have started contacting Open Library regardless of that setting.
- **The configuration guide says what the profile sends to Open Library:** up to five author names per refresh, with results cached for 30 days. Each request carries only a name, but together the names reflect what the reader keeps. So the guide no longer says retrieval sends "nothing about the reader" without qualification.

## What readers will see

After the new `quire-server:latest` is pulled, a profile refresh can include discovery picks: unread books by authors already in the reader's library, each linked to its Open Library page. The Android app already renders them, so no app release is needed.

On a server that still has `openlibrary` in `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_SOURCES`, which is the default, each refresh makes up to 10 requests to Open Library (two per author, one to find the author and one for their works). Results are cached, 30 days for a hit and 24 hours for a miss, so a refresh in the following days usually makes none.

## Worth knowing

Discovery runs one author at a time, as it was designed to. If Open Library hangs, each author waits for `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_RETRIEVAL_TIMEOUT_S` (8 s by default), so up to about 40 s before the model call. That fits the profile's time budget unless the model is also slow and needs its retry. In that case a refresh can hit the server's outer limit and answer 504, which the reader can retry. It needs Open Library to be down and a slow model at the same time, so I've left it as it was designed.

## Testing

- There are two new integration tests. Each keeps the retriever `create_app` wires and serves Open Library and the model from fakes.
  - **The top author's unread work becomes a discovery pick; the owned one does not.** This test fails without the `main.py` change.
  - **With `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_SOURCES=wikipedia`, no Open Library request is made and discovery is empty.** This test fails without the gate in `service.py`.
- Ruff passes, both the version CI installs and the latest.

title: fix(server): 🐛 make three settings do what the configuration guide says
body:
## Why

Writing the configuration guide (#125) meant checking every setting against the code, and a few settings did not do what they said. This PR fixes them, so the guide no longer has to carry "known issue" notes.

## What changes

**The profile refresh limit now takes effect.** `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_PROFILE_REFRESH_DAILY_LIMIT` was read but never handed to the AI service, so readers always got 3 refreshes a day whatever the setting said. `create_app` now passes it on. For example, with the limit set to 5, the sixth refresh of the day gets a 429 saying `limit: 5`. A value of `0` turns the cap off.

**AI source names work in any case, and a misspelled one is no longer silent.**
- Until now, `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_SOURCES=Wikipedia,OpenLibrary` turned retrieval off without a word, while `/ai/v1/config` still listed both sources as enabled.
- The setting is now read in one place (`parse_ai_sources` in `config.py`, replacing two copies of the parsing). That function ignores case and spaces, drops repeats, and keeps only the names retrieval knows.
- An unknown name is ignored with a boot warning that also appears in `GET /health`. Like the other warnings there, it names the variable and never the value, because `/health` is public.
- `/ai/v1/config` and `/ai/v1/health` now report the sources actually in use. `/ai/v1/health` used to show a row that stayed empty forever for a misspelled name.

**The migration step reads the mode switches the way the server does.**
- `scripts/migrate.py` had its own true/false parser that knew only `1/true/yes/on`, and it read the names only in capitals. With `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_ENABLED=y`, the server turned AI on but the migration step skipped the AI tables.
- It now takes both switches from the server's own `get_settings()`. `migrations/env.py` already builds those settings for the database URL, so this adds no new way to fail. An invalid value now stops the migration step with pydantic's message instead of being read as "off".
- The test harness had the same narrow parser for skipping mode-gated tests. It now uses the same settings.

**Stale pointers and comments:**
- The unknown-setting warning points at `docs/configuration.md`, and the leftover "Environment variables" heading in `server/README.md` is gone.
- The Dockerfile and `pyproject.toml` no longer claim the legacy variable prefix is still accepted; nothing accepts it.
- `docs/architecture.md` no longer says native auth with AI in basic mode crashes at boot, and it lists the third AI authenticator.
- `.secrets.baseline` gets the current line number for `config.py`. The old number made pre-commit fail on any commit touching that file.

## What this means for a running server

After merge, `server-ci` publishes a new `quire-server:latest`. Two behaviours change for operators who pull it:
- A profile refresh limit set in `.env` starts to apply.
- A capitalised source name such as `Wikipedia` now turns that source on, where before it was silently off.

A `.env` with an invalid mode value, such as `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_ENABLED=maybe`, used to be read as "off" by the migration step; it now stops the container at the migration step. The server already refused to start with that value, so no working setup breaks. No Android release is cut.

## Testing

- The full server suite passes in full mode on both halves of the work (752 and 750 passed).
- On the combined branch, the changed test files pass in all three CI modes: full 123 passed; sync_only 82 passed, 41 skipped; ai_only 109 passed, 14 skipped.
- The new tests for the refresh limit, `/ai/v1/config` and `/ai/v1/health` fail without the fix.
- Ruff passes, both the version CI installs and the latest. So do pre-commit on the changed files and the rename guard on the added lines.

## Not in this PR

`create_app` never passes `profile_retriever_factory` to the AI service. So the Reader Profile's discovery step (Open Library bibliographies of authors you have finished) always comes back empty in production, although `docs/architecture.md` describes it as working. That fix changes what the profile shows, so it gets its own PR.

Refs #102

title: fix(android): 🐛 read chapters in any encoding, stop HTML chapters turning red, and credit the bundled fonts
body:
#128 got Gutenberg chapters rendering again, and left four reader follow-ups on the list. This PR closes three of them and one more bug found along the way. Each is its own commit. ## Chapters not in UTF-8 now show the text their authors wrote Readium 3.0.0 decodes every chapter as UTF-8 when it injects its CSS and scripts, whatever the chapter declares. So an ISO-8859-1 "café" reached the WebView as "cafï¿½", Shift_JIS text was lost outright, and a UTF-16 chapter failed to load at all (`net::ERR_FAILED`). The fix hooks into Readium's own supported path for transforming resources (`TransformingContainer` with `Resource.map`, in the `onCreatePublication` hook). Only the book's HTML and XHTML documents are wrapped, and `utf8Document` hands each one to Readium in UTF-8. It reads the encoding where the WebView would look: a byte-order mark first, then the XML declaration, then (for documents served as HTML) a `` charset. It rewrites those declarations to say UTF-8. A few details: - **Legacy labels read the way browsers read them.** ISO-8859-1 is read as windows-1252, so its curly quotes survive, and Shift_JIS as windows-31j. - **UTF-16 without a byte-order mark is recognised.** - **Chapters that need no transcoding are left alone.** A chapter already in UTF-8, or in an encoding Java doesn't know, comes back as the same array. Archive entry lengths are untouched, so saved reading positions don't move. The XHTML well-formedness check now reads those transcoded bytes, so its encoding rule shrinks to "is it valid UTF-8". The old Readium round-trip branch is deleted, and `RULES` moves to `xhtml-rules-3` so cached verdicts are recomputed. ## Chapters read by the HTML parser no longer turn red on tap HTML ignores the slash in ``, so Project Gutenberg's anchors stayed open around every paragraph that followed, and the stylesheet's `a:hover` turned the chapter red on the first tap. `closeEmptyElements` rewrites self-closing, non-void elements as pairs (``) in every document served as HTML. That covers both XHTML chapters the relaxer hands to the HTML parser and chapters the book itself declares `text/html`. It follows HTML's tokenizer rules, so it leaves alone: - void elements (`
`, ``); - comments and CDATA; - the contents of `

title: fix(android): 🐛 make quick taps on the page slider land where they tap
body:
## What was wrong

A tap on the reader's page slider could seek to the wrong place if it arrived while the reader was still busy, for example still laying out the chapter the previous tap had jumped to. Sometimes the book jumped to its very start, the cover. Other times the tap was lost and the book stayed where the thumb already was.

The cause is in Compose, not in Quire's code. Material3's slider notes where the finger went down in a task it queues on the main thread, and Compose foundation 1.7 runs that task late. If the finger-up is handled first, the slider has no press position to use.

## What changes

- **Compose BOM 2024.09.02 → 2025.07.00**, which is Compose 1.8.3, the last 1.8 release. Foundation 1.8 notes the press immediately. Material3 stays at 1.3.2.
- **compileSdk 34 → 35 in every module.** Compose 1.8 requires it.
- **Android Gradle Plugin 8.5.2 → 8.6.1**, the first release tested with API 35. It still runs on the current Gradle 8.10.2.
- **CI, CodeQL, the release job and the `dgradle` Docker image** now install the android-35 platform instead of android-34.
- **The licenses screen data** is regenerated. It picks up Compose 1.8.3, AndroidX patch releases (lifecycle 2.8.7, emoji2 1.4.0, profileinstaller 1.4.0) and jspecify (Apache 2.0), which Compose now pulls in.

## What does not change

**targetSdk stays at 34**, so the app behaves the same at runtime. Moving to 35 would force edge-to-edge layout and deserves its own PR. The window bar colour setters in `ReaderScreen` become deprecated at API 35. They keep working at targetSdk 34, and that is the only new compiler warning.

**Why not the latest Compose?** The current release (1.12, BOM 2026.09.00) needs compileSdk 37 and AGP 9.1. That is a much larger migration than this fix needs.

## Checks

**New unit test, `ReaderBottomBarTest`.** It taps the middle of the slider with the finger-down and finger-up back to back.
- On foundation 1.7 it fails with the reported symptom: expected 0.5, got 0.0.
- On 1.8.3 it passes.
- It needs a `StandardTestDispatcher`. The test rule's default dispatcher runs queued tasks on the spot, which hid the bug; the test passed on 1.7 until I changed that.

**Full local run.** All 1354 unit tests pass, lint passes, and `assembleDebug` and `assembleRelease` both build.

**Emulator stress test** (Pixel 10, Pride and Prejudice). Each round taps the slider near the start, then taps its middle 0.15 s later. Both builds come from the same main commit.

| Build | Middle taps that landed at 49% | Taps lost |
|---|---|---|
| main (Compose 1.7.2) | 42 of 50 | 8 (stayed at 8%, where the first tap had gone) |
| this branch (Compose 1.8.3) | 50 of 50 | 0 |

With a 0.5 s gap, neither build lost a tap in 30 rounds, so the bug needs the app to be genuinely busy when the tap arrives.

title: fix(android): 🐛 draw OpenDyslexic's real italic and bold
body:
## What was wrong

Quire offers OpenDyslexic as a reader font, but only its regular face shipped: the copy bundled inside Readium. So every italic or bold word was faked. The web view slanted or thickened the regular letters, which distorts exactly the letter shapes this font is designed around, for the readers who chose it for that reason.

## What changes

- **Quire now bundles OpenDyslexic's real italic, bold and bold italic.** They are the 2.001 files from the archived `antijingoist/open-dyslexic` repo at commit 03aa683. That is the same release and the same repo as the regular face Readium ships (byte-identical), so the four faces form one consistent family.
- **They are declared under Readium's own family name.** Readium adds its regular face to the same family afterwards, so the page gets all four faces and nothing is duplicated.
- **Why not OpenDyslexic 3?** It is the maintained release and is under the SIL Open Font License, but its letters run up to 31% wider than 2.001. An italic word from it would look like a different font in the middle of a line.

## License and size

- The three files carry the same terms as the regular face that already ships: the Bitstream Vera license plus CC BY 3.0. This adds no new terms to the app.
- The terms ship beside the fonts as `LICENSE-OpenDyslexic.txt`.
- `NOTICE` and the in-app licenses screen now describe the whole family.
- The APK grows by about 191 KB.

## Checks

- `ReaderFontsTest`:
  - now expects OpenDyslexic among the declared families, with a real face for every style;
  - a new test asserts that Quire declares only the three non-regular faces;
  - a new test asserts that each face reports the same font version as Readium's regular. I checked that this test fails when a face doesn't match: with a 3.008 file swapped in, it failed and named the file. So a future Readium upgrade that moves its regular face to OpenDyslexic 3 fails here, not on the page.
- The full unit suite and lint pass locally (1353 tests, no failures).
- On the Pixel 10 emulator with Pride and Prejudice, I asked the web view which font files drew the text:
  - **Before (main):** italic and bold text were both drawn with `OpenDyslexic-Regular`.
  - **After:** italic is drawn with `OpenDyslexic-Italic` and bold with `OpenDyslexic-Bold`. An inserted bold italic sample is drawn with `OpenDyslexic-BoldItalic`.
  - The preface of this edition is set in italic and now shows the real italic design; the book titles inside it stay upright.

title: fix(android): 🐛 keep the reader controls up until the reader dismisses them
body:
## What went wrong

Dragging the page slider sometimes seemed to send the book to the wrong place: a reader aimed at the middle of a book and landed on the page before the one they were on. The slider was not at fault. The reader controls hide themselves 2.5 s after they appear, so a reader who opened them and took a moment to reach for the slider found them gone just as their finger came down. The tap then fell through to the page. The slider sits low on the left, inside the "previous page" third of the screen, so the book turned back one page.

## What changes

- **Controls the reader opens stay open.** A centre tap now shows the controls until the reader's next tap, with no timer. The 2.5 s auto-hide only applies to the reveal the reader sees when a book first opens.
- **A tap on the page while the controls are showing closes them, and does not turn the page.** With the controls up, a tap that misses a control was almost certainly aimed at one, so the page should not move. With the controls hidden, left and right taps turn pages exactly as before.
- **The auto-hide clock on book open now starts once the book has actually opened.** A large book that took a few seconds to parse used to lose its controls before its first page appeared.

## Checks

- A new `ReaderChromeTest` covers both parts: a reader-opened reveal no longer auto-hides, and a page tap with the controls showing toggles them instead of turning the page.
- The full unit suite passes locally (1351 tests, no failures).
- On the Pixel 10 emulator:
  - controls opened with a centre tap were still up after 14 s;
  - a left-third tap with the controls up hid them and left the page pixel-identical;
  - with the controls hidden, left and right taps still turn pages;
  - a slider press 5 s after the reveal jumped to 50%.

## Not in this PR

There is a separate slider bug: a tap exactly at 0% does not register. It comes from Compose foundation 1.7 and is fixed from Compose BOM 2025.04.00 on. That upgrade needs compileSdk 35 and probably a newer Android Gradle Plugin, so it is a separate decision.

title: fix(android): 🐛 drop the phone's saved copy when an insight is invalidated
body:
## The button did nothing

A reader generated an insight for a book while the server's retrieval sources were switched off, so the model made the
insight up. They opened Inspect Insight, tapped "Invalidate cached insight" and confirmed. Their server logged
`POST /ai/v1/insights/invalidate 200 OK` and deleted its copy, yet the app went on showing the same made-up insight.
Force-closing the app, Android's "Clear cache" and Settings "Refresh insights" did not remove it either, and after the
invalidate their server never saw another request for that book.

The reason: the phone keeps its own saved copy of every insight and reads that copy before it ever asks the server.
Invalidate told the server to delete its row and deliberately left the phone's copy in place, expecting a later sync to
replace it. Nothing ever does: the server row is gone, so there is nothing to sync, and a sync only pulls rows newer than
what the phone already has. Android's "Clear cache" does not touch the app database. So the button has never worked for
anyone.

## What changes

**Invalidate now drops the phone's copy too.** After the server confirms the delete, the app removes every saved insight
for that book: every model, prompt version, tone and language, whether the row was filed under the book's metadata id or
its content hash. Removing all variants is on purpose. When the phone is offline it falls back to "any saved insight for
this book", and leaving an older variant behind would let that fallback bring a discarded insight straight back. In
practice: tap Invalidate, go back to the book, and the app asks the server afresh, which generates a new insight with
whatever sources are on now.

**A server that has nothing counts as success; a real failure changes nothing.** If the server answers 404 (nothing
stored for this book, or AI not enabled on that server), that is already the state the reader asked for, so the phone's
copy is dropped as well. On a network error, 401, 5xx or anything else, the phone keeps its copy and the audit screen still
says "Couldn't invalidate", so the reader never ends up with a phone that claims the insight is gone while the server
still has it.

**The audit screen's own 404 handling is gone.** It used to treat a 404 as success itself. With the repository doing that
one layer down, that branch could no longer run, so it and its test are removed.

**The insight request keeps an author the library already knows.** When a book's EPUB metadata names no author, the
request used to go out with a title only, which is what the reporter's Open Library lookups showed. The library row often
does know the author, because it can come from the OPDS feed entry or a library restore rather than the EPUB. The app now
uses that author when the EPUB has none; an author in the EPUB still wins.

## Tests

- Repository: invalidating a book with a saved insight makes the next read go to the server and come back empty when the
  server has nothing; a 404 on invalidate still clears the phone's copy; a 500 or a dropped connection leaves the copy in place and surfaces the
  error.
- Database: the new delete removes a book's rows filed under either identity and every style variant, spares another
  book, and a missing metadata id never matches unrelated rows.
- Metadata: an EPUB without an author takes the library's; an EPUB author wins; no EPUB metadata falls back to the
  library row; a blank library author is never sent.

## What does not change

- Other devices are not told about the deletion. A second phone keeps its saved copy until its reader invalidates there
  too; syncing deletions between devices is separate work.
- Settings "Refresh insights" behaves as before.
- A sync that is already running at the moment of the tap can write the old insight back to the phone, because it
  fetched the row before the server deleted it. Tapping Invalidate again clears it for good. Making the two wait for
  each other is a small follow-up.
- No server changes and no wording changes in the UI.

Refs #102

Invalidate now removes the insight from the phone as well as the server, so the button finally does what it says.

title: fix(android): 🐛 cancel the HTTP call when its coroutine is cancelled
body:
## The story

Last week the app learned to wait as long as the server may take when generating an insight, sized from what the server advertises, instead of giving up after a minute while the server was still working. That fixed the visible problem and quietly created two smaller ones.

The first is that the waiting was unconditional. Every request ran a blocking call on an IO thread, so a reader who opened a book, saw the spinner and changed their mind left that thread and its socket pinned until the wait expired. That used to mean a minute. It can now mean ten.

The second is that a reader-profile refresh borrows the insight budget, although the server caps a profile refresh far lower. The app therefore waited several times longer than the server would ever take.

## What changes in practice

- Every request in the AI client now goes through one small helper that ties the HTTP call to the coroutine that asked for it. Leaving the screen cancels the call, and the thread and socket are released immediately rather than at the end of the wait.
- A response that arrives in the instant between the cancellation and the callback is closed rather than dropped, so the connection it holds is released too. That race is the one case a naive version of this helper leaks, and it is the only case where the helper could make things worse instead of better.
- The profile refresh sizes its wait from `profile_timeout_s` when the server advertises it, and falls back to today's behaviour against a server that does not. The field is optional on purpose: either side can ship first.

Nothing changes for a reader who waits for an insight to arrive. Exception mapping, quota wording and the rule that a rate limit never reads as a provider failure are all untouched.

## Notes for review

Checked on an emulator against a server whose provider was made to hang, so that only the app could end the call. The server was willing to wait five minutes, the provider ten times longer than the measurement window, and the app itself ten minutes.

| What the reader does | What happens to the connection |
|---|---|
| Stays on the screen | Still open after 45 seconds, as it should be |
| Leaves the screen | Released about 5 seconds later |

Without this change the same connection would have been held for the full ten minutes. The delay before release is the navigation and view-model teardown, not the network layer.

- A unit test covers the cancellation path with a mock server and asserts the call ends promptly rather than at the timeout. A second test for the closed-response race was written and then removed: forcing that race from inside the dispatcher thread destabilised other tests in the same module, and an intermittent failure elsewhere is a worse trade than reviewing this one carefully. The fix itself is the documented API for exactly this case in the coroutines version the project pins.
- The app-module test that failed in an earlier run of the full task passed on the final run, twice, and is the order-dependent flake this repo already knows about. Nothing here touches that module.
- Verified on the branch: full test task green, debug APK assembles, and the behaviour above on a device.

Refs #102

title: fix(server): 🐛 let the provider enforce the insight schema
body:
## The story

Phillip's second traceback on #102 turned out not to be a timeout. `llama3.2:1b` answered fast, and what it answered with was the JSON Schema itself: `$defs`, `properties`, `title`, `type`. The blank form, not a filled-in one, twice in a row.

That is a direct consequence of how the client asked. It sent `response_format={"type": "json_object"}`, meaning "any JSON object at all", and pasted the schema into the system prompt as text, on the theory that not every local runtime could enforce a schema. That theory was true when it was written. A one-billion-parameter model handed a schema as text hands it straight back.

## What changes in practice

- The schema now rides in `response_format={"type": "json_schema", ...}`, so the provider constrains the answer itself. Ollama and llama.cpp have supported this for a while, and it is the difference between asking a small model nicely and not giving it the option. The schema leaves the prompt, which also makes the prompt considerably shorter.
- A provider that does not know the mode says so with a 4xx that names the parameter. The client then falls back once to the old shape, schema inlined in the prompt, and keeps that shape for the rest of the process. One extra request per deploy, then nothing.
- A genuine rejection is never downgraded. The downgrade needs a parameter-complaint status code and a body that names the parameter, both at once. Bad credentials and unknown models match neither and still raise as before, with tests pinning each case.
- The retry log line no longer carries the model's answer. A pydantic `ValidationError` stringifies with `input_value=...`, a slice of whatever the provider sent, and that was going into the operator log at INFO. It now logs the error class and a count. The retry message sent back to the model still carries the full error, because that is what makes the retry work.

Nothing changes for a deploy whose model already produces good cards, beyond a shorter prompt. A deploy on a provider without schema support behaves exactly as it does today after one probe request.

## Notes for review

Checked end to end against a local server and a stub provider that records what it was asked for, rather than only in unit tests:

| What the provider does | What the server sends | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Answers normally | Schema in `response_format`, not in the prompt | Insight returned, system prompt 4110 characters |
| Refuses the mode | Same, then falls back to `json_object` with the schema pasted | Fallback prompt 11128 characters, clean 502 when that is refused too |
| Answers normally afterwards | Straight to `json_object`, no second probe | Downgrade remembered for the process |

The prompt is about two thirds shorter when the provider holds the schema, which is worth having on its own: a small local model on a CPU spends that prompt before it writes a single token, and shortening it is the first thing the troubleshooting section of the README tells people to try.

- `strict: true` against OpenAI itself will most likely be refused on the first call, because pydantic's `model_json_schema()` does not emit `additionalProperties: false` and does not mark every field required. The refusal names `response_format`, so the client downgrades and behaves as it does today, at the cost of one request per process. Rewriting the schema into strict form means walking `$defs` and forcing every property required with null unions, which is a real chunk of code and its own risk, so it is not in this PR. Worth a follow-up if OpenAI-backed deploys matter.
- The generic 4xx hint used to tell operators that some providers reject `response_format=json_object`. Reaching that hint now means both shapes were refused, so naming one of them sent people looking in the wrong place. It points at the provider logs, the model and the key instead. That is the third commit.
- Verified on the branch: ruff clean, 633 tests pass in full mode, 535 pass with 98 skipped in the AI-only matrix cell.

Refs #102

title: fix(server): 🐛 honor every .env setting and warn on misconfiguration
body:
## The story

Phillip set up the full-stack compose with a local Ollama and got "Couldn't generate insights (500)" with nothing to go on (#102). Three of the causes were ours: the compose files forwarded an allowlist of variables so several documented settings never reached the container, an empty `${VAR:-}` fallback counted as "set", and AI enabled with no provider booted without a word.

## What changes in practice

- Both compose files load `.env` wholesale through `env_file`. The `environment:` block keeps only what the topology decides (database URL, in-network calibre-web in the full stack), and the docs now say that a `.env` line for those two names is ignored. The minimal compose refuses to start without `QUIRE_SERVER_CWA_BASE_URL` instead of booting a server nobody can log in to. `host.docker.internal` resolves on Linux too, so a host-side Ollama works from the container.
- Empty or whitespace `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_BASE_URL`, `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_MODEL`, `QUIRE_SERVER_AI_API_KEY` count as unset.
- At boot the server logs `event=config.warning` for each unknown `QUIRE_SERVER_*` variable (from the environment or from the `.env` a locally run server reads itself), for AI enabled without a provider, for a provider URL without `/v1`, and for both modes off. Warnings name variables and never echo values. `GET /health` repeats the list under `warnings`, so `curl /health` is now the first debugging step.
- `.env.example` is retiered and every line is tagged; the README reference lists every setting in four tables.
- A unit test fails whenever the docs or compose files mention a variable the server does not read, the README misses a setting, or a compose file stops loading `.env`. The test suite ignores a developer's own `server/.env`.

## Things to know before upgrading

- Settings now have to live in `.env`. Variables exported only in the shell (`QUIRE_SERVER_AI_ENABLED=false docker compose up`) used to be interpolated into the container; `env_file` reads the file only, so they are no longer forwarded.
- Docker Compose v2.24.0 or newer is required for the long `env_file` syntax. With the minimal `docker-compose.yml`, `.env` must exist for every compose command, because that file requires `QUIRE_SERVER_CWA_BASE_URL`; the full stack still starts without one.
- The server container now receives every line of `.env`, including the compose-only ones such as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and `PUID`. The server ignores them, but they are visible in that container's environment, so keep unrelated secrets out of the file.

Nothing else changes for a deployment whose `.env` already worked: the same values reach the server, plus a possible warning line.

Closes #104

title: fix(resource): prove the body the sender hashed, and guard the hashmap
body:
Two SPEC §10 conformance gaps. Both were fixed on `fix/resource-spec-adherence` (2026-05-19) and that branch was never merged; these are **re-derived from `SPEC.md`**, not cherry-picked.

Opened as a PR rather than pushed to master: it is wire-touching, 1.2.117 just shipped, and per `playbook.md` §5 a self-round-trip cannot validate this class of change — both ends drift identically. It wants a look against a spec-compliant peer.

## 1. RESOURCE_PRF was hashed over the wrong bytes (§10.2 step 5 / §10.8)

§10.2 step 5 computes the sender's `expected_proof = SHA256(plaintext || hash)` over *"the original uncompressed plaintext — the caller's input, **including any metadata prefix from step 1**"*. §10.8 orders the receiver identically: step 5 hashes the body, step 6 peels metadata off **afterwards**, purely as a delivery concern.

`assemble()` returns the metadata-**stripped** body when the ADV's `x` flag is set, and `LinkResourceReceiver` passed that return value straight into `buildProofPayload`. So any resource carrying metadata got a proof over the wrong bytes. The sender compares bytewise to its `expected_proof`, rejects, and retransmits the whole resource until its watchdog cancels — it fails like a flaky link, not like a wrong hash.

Not a hypothetical shape: metadata is what upstream NomadNet `/file/` responses carry (`Node.py:128-141`), which this client requests via `fetchNomadFile`.

**Fix.** `assemble()` captures the metadata-inclusive body into `proofPlaintext` after the integrity check and before the strip; `buildProofPayload` reads it from there. Dropping the parameter is the point, not a tidy-up — the only caller had the stripped body in hand, so the wrong bytes were reachable by construction.

**Mutation-verified.** Reverting the capture turns exactly the new metadata test red and leaves the others green. That asymmetry is also why this survived since May: with no metadata the two arrays are the same object, so the common path was always correct and the bug was invisible to every self-round-trip.

## 2. The §10.2 step 7 hashmap collision guard was missing

A 4-byte map_hash repeat within `COLLISION_GUARD_SIZE` makes the colliding part un-placeable — the receiver disambiguates an inbound part only inside that window (§10.6), and a part it cannot place is dropped silently, so the transfer stalls looking like an unresponsive peer. Upstream detects this at construction and regenerates the random hash.

The sender now does too, capped at `MAX_COLLISION_RETRIES = 8`. The retry rebuilds the whole segment rather than just the map, because the random hash salts the chunk hashes, the integrity hash and the outer prefix alike. `hashmapHasGuardCollision` is O(n) via a last-seen map keyed on the packed 4 bytes; a pairwise scan would cost ~3.6M comparisons per send on a `MAX_RESOURCE_PARTS` segment.

Odds are ~1e-4 on a full ~1 MiB segment, so the cap is not a throughput concern — it makes a pathological body fail loudly at construction, naming the reason, instead of looping.

Tests pin the window boundary: a repeat exactly `COLLISION_GUARD_SIZE` apart is **not** a collision (the receiver's search is `< consecutive + GUARD`, so it stays disambiguable); one index closer is.

## Verification

- `:shared:testDebugUnitTest` and `:androidApp:testDebugUnitTest` both green.
- Mutation check as described above.
- **Not** verified against a live spec-compliant peer.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_01Pu4nRMJbPenrt4gpBp5uPV

title: fix(nodes): focus the search field when revealed (#44)
body:
Fixes #44 — reported by @bergie on 1.2.91 (Galaxy S25 Ultra / Android 16).

## Symptom (verified against the code, not just the report)
Tapping the Search icon in the Nodes / contact list reveals the search
`OutlinedTextField` (`searchActive` toggle) but doesn't focus it, so it
takes a second tap to start typing. `NodesScreen.kt` has no
`FocusRequester` anywhere, which is the cause. The Messages-tab search
field is always visible (not toggle-revealed), so it's unaffected.

when the field appears (inside the `if (searchActive)` block so it
re-fires on each reveal; `requestFocus` wrapped in `runCatching` for the
fast-recompose "not attached" race). One tap now reveals the field,
places the cursor, and raises the keyboard.

title: fix(cache): Don't refetch a watcher for the asynchronous write of its own initial fetch
body:
With `writeToCacheAsynchronously`, the cache write of a response is launched rather than awaited, so it lands after the response has been emitted - and, for the initial fetch of a `watch()`, after the watcher has subscribed to the cache. The watcher was then notified of a change it had just made itself, and refetched to emit data the caller already had.

A synchronous write cannot do that: it publishes before its response is emitted, which is before the watcher subscribes, which is the whole reason the last initial response is withheld until the subscription exists.

The cache write now reports the exact set of keys it is about to publish to the request that asked for it, and the watcher drops the event carrying that set. Sets are matched by identity, so each publication is its own event and a change published by anyone else - including one that touches the same keys - still notifies the watcher. Nothing is lost by dropping it: the response the write stored has already been emitted, and any other write that merged into the same records publishes an event of its own.

Only the initial fetch reports what it publishes. A refetch runs while subscribed whether writes are asynchronous or not, so being notified of its own write is not specific to this flag and is left as is.

Fixes: https://github.com/apollographql/apollo-kotlin-normalized-cache/issues/375
